#2696. 5 things to watch when the Cowboys play the Titans

The Dallas Cowboys walk into Sunday in desperate need of a get-right game after opening up the floodgates to the San Francisco 49ers last week. A visit from the terrible Tennessee Titans looks like the perfect team to oblige. Tied for the worst record in the league at 1-8, the Titans have their own problems and could offer some relief for a team that is hanging on to playoff hopes and chasing the New York Giants for the NFC East crown.

Of course, with the way the Cowboys have played this season, even a matchup against a one-win team carries enough nervous energy to keep us from feeling comfortable. Let's face it, we're always on pins and needles. That is, until they puncture through and rip apart our spirits.

But that's not going to happen this week, right? Let's hope not. Here are five things to watch when the Cowboys host the Titans on Sunday.

After giving up 46 points last week to the 49ers, head coach Brian Schottenheimer said enough is enough and stripped defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling responsibilities, handing the reins to veteran senior assistant Mike Pettine. What will this defense look like under Pettine's control? He hasn't called plays since 2020 with the Packers, so everyone will be watching to see how his tendencies change and whether we finally see any real improvement on that side of the ball.

Keep in mind, this is a bottom-five scoring offense in Tennessee, so even a good showing on Sunday might not tell us much about whether the unit is actually improving. However, a bad showing against one of the worst teams in football could allow morale to sink even lower than it already is. Does anyone else know how to call plays?

While on the surface this seems like it should be a breather for a struggling Cowboys' defense, let's not count our chickens. The Titans are starting to show some signs of life after a miserable beginning to the season. Over their first five games, the Titans never scored more than 20 points, including three agonizing outings where they failed to clear 10 points. Lately, though, they have flipped the script by scoring over 20 points in each of their last four games.

A big reason for the turnaround is the improved play of last year's first overall pick, Cam Ward, who is coming off the first 300-yard passing game of his career just a couple of weeks ago. He has also strung together back-to-back games with multiple touchdown passes after failing to do it once over his first seven starts. The Cowboys defense simply cannot catch a break, as this struggling unit now faces a previously inept offense that is suddenly heating up. The Cowboys defense doesn't do so well with heat.

Tony Pollard will play his first game against the Cowboys since leaving in free agency in 2024, and he brings plenty of momentum back to Arlington. Pollard is having a career year in Tennessee, averaging a career-high 69.8 rushing yards per game while on pace to become the first player in NFL history drafted in the fourth round or later to record five 1,000-yard rushing seasons.

On Sunday, he faces a Cowboys defense allowing a league-worst 154 rushing yards per game, including two games already in November where they've allowed over 200 yards. Pollard would love nothing more than to creep closer to the 1,000-yard mark with a huge afternoon against his former team.

While the defense remains a giant question mark, one thing that should not be a mystery is the Cowboys' offense. There is absolutely no excuse for them not to roll right through the Titans' defense on Sunday. No team in the NFL allows more passing yards than Tennessee this season, as they are surrendering an average of 267 yards per game through the air.

Dak Prescott and company just put up 40 points against a good 49ers defense last week, so they should be able to light up the Titans without thinking too much about it, right? Let's certainly hope so. Anything short of a dominant performance against this secondary might mean they should consider handing the offensive play-calling responsibilities to someone else, too. Just kidding. Sort of.

Pollard isn't the only familiar face returning to AT&T Stadium, as special teams coordinator John Fassel makes his way back after spending five seasons in Dallas. Alongside him is Titans defensive line coach Aaron Whitecotton, who coached with the Cowboys last season. Dallas strongly considered keeping him around, even interviewing him for the defensive coordinator position, before ultimately going with Parker.

Despite trading star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, Tennessee is still able to generate pressure without having to blitz, opening the door to create some real issues for the Cowboys' offense if they show up complacent. You better believe that Whitecotton knows exactly how to attack the Cowboys offensive line, and it could spell trouble if Dallas isn't sharp.

#2695. Tornado, USF can't stop Florida Atlantic football from victory

BOCA RATON — In the longest game in program history, Florida Atlantic displayed defensive dominance to beat South Florida for the first time since 2023.

Two weather delays, a tornado warning - and an actual tornado that could be seen from the stadium - and after almost six hours, the Owls finally defeated USF at home for the first time via a 35-14 victory.

FAU (7-4, 4-3) forced two turnovers and limited USF (6-5, 2-5) to zero points in the first half of the American Conference game to mark the first time the Owls went 6-0 at home in a season.

"It was awesome to see," FAU coach Zach Kittley said. "I told our guys after the first (weather delay), you know, we've lived this with some lightning delays, and we've had to go sit inside for 30 minutes to an hour, then we gotta flip the script.

More weather news: Billie Jean King Cup plagued by thunderstorms, tornado watch

"You gotta get back outside and get going.  And so we've done this before. Our guys handled it like pros. Coming out of that long halftime, I thought we dominated the third quarter in a great fashion. We were like really just clicking on all cylinders and that was great to see."

It was the second week in a row that FAU's football team was plagued by non-game factors; last week, the team charter flight was grounded on Friday by an FAA announcement and the Owls had to fly to Tulsa on game day.

On Saturday, it was a performance to remember on Senior Day as the Owls held the Bulls to 14 points and under 100 rushing yards, the first time FAU has done that since late September.

Here are three takeaways from the victory against USF.

Senior quarterback Caden Veltkamp was once again efficient for the Owls, throwing for 386 yards and four touchdowns.

In what potentially could be Veltkamp's last time playing in Boca Raton, he was a little emotional before the game.

"I was the last one to go out so I had a lot of time to sit there and think about it," Veltkamp said. "The way that Kittley brought me in (transfer portal) , it always felt like family. Everybody in our building, and our coaching staff, and everybody on our team. I could not be more grateful for my time here at FAU.

"It's been everything that I wanted it to be so far. I am super proud of what we have accomplished and I'm excited for the last two (games)."

Veltkamp uncorked a 36-yard touchdown pass to tight end A.J. Johnson to get the Owls on the board. Early in the second quarter, he threw a 16-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver Kelby Valsin for a 14-0 lead.

After the weather delay, the Owls' came out firing on all cylinders in the second half. Veltkamp connected with Easton Messer for his 18th touchdown of the season, extending FAU's lead to 21-0.

The duo wasn't done. Late in the third quarter Veltkamp connected with Messer for his 33rd passing touchdown of the season and Messer's second of the day, breaking FAU's single-season passing touchdown record.

Messer came into Saturday's game as questionable with an upper body injury. Alhough he went through pregame warmups, he wasn't on the field for the Owls' first two offensive series.

Messer was in and out of the lineup, but his injury did not limit FAU's production offensively.

Valsin led all receivers with 12 catches for 112 yards, and Dom Henry had an impactful day with six catches for 106 yards. Valsin also amassed over 1,000 receiving yards on the season, marking the first time in program history that FAU has had two 1,000 yard receivers (Messer & Valsin).

Messer finished with four catches for 64 yards and the two scores, and knew his teammates would pick up the slack with him being limited.

"Even on the first drive, I knew these guys were gonna be able to take care of business, but it just got to the point where sitting over there, you know, just didn't feel right.  So I had to pop in a little bit," Messer explained.

All season long, FAU's struggles defensively have been its Achilles heel. The Owls especially struggled against the run, allowing 238 rushing yards per game, second worst mark in the country entering Saturday's home finale. FAU also was allowing 228 passing yards per game, third worst in the conference.

On Saturday, the defense proved it can stifle a quality opponent. USF came into Saturday scoring 27 points per game, and the Owls held the Bulls scoreless in the first half. Additionally, the Bulls hadn't thrown an interception this season, but FAU changed that early in the first quarter, where a tipped pass bounced into defensive end Josh Robert's hands.

The Owls also forced a fumble in the first half after a big hit from safety Bo Simpson-Nealy and they brought pressure to the Bulls all game, disallowing USF's offense from getting into a rhythm. Simpson-Nealy spoke about how the home environment helped the defense hit its stride. The defense had four sacks, two on fourth downs, and five tackles for a loss.

"At home it's just different. There's different energy, it's a different environment," he said. "I feel amazing that we're undefeated at home, and we made history."

This article originally appeared on Palm Beach Post: Tornado, USF can't stop Florida Atlantic football from victory

#2693. Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez named unanimous American League MVP after nearly winning 2026 Triple Crown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez has won the 2026 American League MVP, the BBWAA announced Thursday night.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing AL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Alvarez, 29, bounced back from an injury-riddled disaster in 2025, during which he only played in 48 games. This time around, he avoided the IL and appeared in 158 games. He hit .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+) with 34 doubles, a triple, 42 home runs, 106 RBI, 105 runs and 6.8 WAR. He made a late run at the Triple Crown, missing out by one home run and seven RBI. He did lead the majors in all three triple slash categories, though, leading in average by five points, on-base percentage by a whopping 42 points -- he led the majors in walks -- and 31 points in slugging percentage. Add the latter two and his OPS victory was 90 points -- 1.033 to second place's .943 (National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong).

The only players in MLB history to lead the majors in all three triple slash categories:

Alvarez becomes just the third Astros player to win MVP after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

Rays third baseman Junior Caminero finished in second. At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. came in third. This is now his fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

#2690. Wolves 104, Grizzlies 99: Defense Downs the Bear

Basketball is a funny thing. One night, the world is obsessed with your offense-capping defensive stalwart and the next you're holding the number one offense in all of basketball to 99 points while that aforementioned rim protector has an incredible game (and still missed some layups).

In a game in which they looked dominant throughout, the Minnesota Timberwolves taught the Memphis Grizzlies that there is joy in being a young, upstart team, but it is still incredibly hard to face off with a capable team on a random Saturday with some of your best players absent.

No, luckily, the Wolves have seemingly learned this lesson.

Minnesota's five-point margin is significantly smaller than it likely should be after the Grizzlies outscored them by 12 in the fourth quarter. Don't be fooled, this was functionally a wire to wire victory.

The Wolves employed a bit of a platoon plan on offense tonight, spreading usage to each of the starters and allowing Jonathan Kuminga, Jaden McDaniels, and Ayo Dosunmu to all turn in impressive point totals. This Wolves team just keeps showing up and playing well in a way that could not be further from what Wolves fans are used to. Memphis leaned on Cedric Coward and Most Improved Player frontrunner Ty Jerome, but struggled to do much of anything until a garbage time run.

This was a game that put the floor of the Wolves on display more than its ceiling. This was a close win against an admittedly great team with clear weaknesses. If we're going to start there, with the two-in-one ceiling capper and floor raiser, there's only one man to talk about.

Look, the discourse surrounding Rudy Gobert does make sense. He may be the single greatest floor-raising defensive presence since Tim Duncan or Hakeem Olajuwon, but he also makes those two look like Moses combined with prime Escalade on offense.

(And yes, folks, going from being a bad catcher of the basketball to a stone-handed anomaly who is putting up 40ish% on layups is, in fact, a major regression).

Tonight was one of those nights where everything looked decent for Gobert, even if he only scored seven points. Considering the state of the timeline over the past few days – if you are lobbying for Myles Turner, you live in a 2K fanfiction – it was nice to have a reminder of what a *good* Gobert game can look like.

Anytime Minnesota has a great defensive game, everyone will place the flowers at Gobert's feet. This is, after all, exactly what he was supposed to do here. However, the hand-wave of "Gobert was great" doesn't give him his full deserved credit. Memphis did not look at the rim all game. That meant that by the time they got hot, they were in two deep of a hole to get out of.

The man may be an absolute deadbeat, have the health/food knowledge of a yule log (maybe one that's worm-eaten too), but he is an absurdly game-altering talent.

It may be impossible to replace him, and no one seems willing to give up anything of value for him. At that point, it seems the future holds a lot of floor-raising. After tonight, that sounds pretty perfect.

Five different players hit double digits for Minnesota tonight. Jaden McDaniels (25 points on 11/17 from the field), Ayo Dosunmu (19 points), Jonathan Kuminga (16 points on 6/9 shooting), LaMelo Ball (on 50% from the field after a bad stretch), and TJ Shannon Jr. each scored over 10 points, and together they provided all but 17 points in this game.

The headliner is a hyper-efficient Jaden McDaniels game, but it feels like he is destined to never truly empty the clip, instead opting to be a capable third option no matter who he is sharing the court with. Some days, he's the number three guy to Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball; other days, he's letting Greg Monroe initiate the offense while on a 10-day. Tonight, however, he deferred to Kuminga and Ayo as the two turned defense into offense.

However, the real storyline is TJ Shannon, who continues to rise up the depth chart (much to my personal surprise) as another change-of-pace option in attacking the rim. His 15 points in 26 minutes comes after he looked to have found some confidence and comfort in his last few games.

There was a tweet from a few weeks ago that sticks with me about this team. It said the Wolves have on of the best 1-9s in the league, but have the most garbage 10- 15s as well.

Depth is so hard to really pull off, but the Wolves have the right kind of options. Instead of playing around waiting for a loophole, Minnesota just straight up outperformed and outdelivered what the Grizzlies could do off the bench

The Wolves will face off against Julius Randle and the Brooklyn Nets on Monday evening as the two former allies will fight over who deserves their low ppg elbow touches. Considering all of this is about raising the floor, the 3-12 Nets probably wish they pursued Gobert instead of Randle.

#2688. CFP chances after Week 12: Who has best chances to make 12-team bracket?

Two weeks from now, the College Football Playoff selection committee will unveil the official 12-team bracket.

There remains plenty of flux until that moment, as teams battle for spots in conference championship games across the country. Others sit on the bubble for at-large bids and postseason seeding ahead of Selection Sunday on Sunday, Dec. 6.

Georgia looks well-positioned to be the top overall seed in the third and final iteration of the 12-team bracket, with Kirby Smart's squad sitting at 10-1 overall and already clinching a spot in the SEC Championship game for the sixth consecutive season.

FLOP 10: Big Ten talks B1G game, but CFP disaster leaves conference leading Flop 10

Week 12 delivered several results that could shake up the College Football Playoff picture, setting the stage for further movement when the selection committee unveils its fourth CFP top 25 rankings Tuesday, Nov. 24.

Among the most significant results from Week 12, a slate that offered few marquee matchups but plenty of surprises, were losses by Indiana and UCLA. The Hoosiers fell to Washington in overtime, while the Bruins were upset by Michigan in triple overtime. Those setbacks have opened the door to a startling possibility: the Big Ten, a conference that has produced the past three national champions, could wind up with just one team in this season's playoff field.

So, going into the final week of the regular season, who has the best percentage chances of hearing their name called in the official 12-team bracket in just 14 days?

Both Georgia and Utah are near 100% locks to make the College Football Playoff following Week 12 using ESPN's FPI metric. Notre Dame follows the Bulldogs and Utes at 98.6% after the Fighting Irish picked up their fourth straight win, beating SMU 24-3 in Week 12.

It is worth noting that ESPN's FPI playoff metrics can swing dramatically over the next two weeks. Take Indiana, the defending national champion, as an example. The Hoosiers currently have an 86.9% chance of making 12-team College Football Playoff, but that outlook changes significantly depending on how the season finishes. If Indiana rebounds from its Week 12 loss to Washington by beating Purdue in Week 13 but fails to secure a spot in the Big Ten championship game, its playoff odds drop to 42%. Reaching Indianapolis will require help elsewhere, with the Hoosiers needing results involving Iowa, Oregon and UCLA.

That's just one of several scenarios using ESPN's playoff predictor that can make booking tickets for the postseason either a safe or risky investment before Selection Sunday hits.

#2687. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2686. Now with an MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the path for an all-time great career. Where could he stack up?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The MVP winners were revealed Thursday evening and, unsurprisingly, the runaway unanimous winner in the National League was Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs.

Crow-Armstrong had an all-time great regular season, which is what the annual Baseball Writers' Association of America award honors. He hit .280/.372/.570 with stellar defense, led the league in home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and massively upgraded his on-base skills. Now, just a few months shy of his 25th birthday, he has an MVP to his name.

So what's next? To answer that, we'll look backwards.

Since integration, only eight center fielders have posted at least 8.0 WAR in a season age-25 or younger: Willie Mays, Mickey Mantle, Willie Davis, César Cedeño, Ken Griffey Jr., Andruw Jones, Mike Trout and PCA. The only ones to top PCA's 9.8 were Mays, Mantle and Trout. If we went back to pre-integration, Tris Speaker and Ty Cobb were the only others who bested PCA here.

Willie Davis was an inconsistent hitter through his age-23 season but had flashed a nice power-speed combo. Sound familiar? That gaudy 8.4 WAR total in 1964, though, was driven largely by monster defensive metrics. Davis hit .294/.316/.413 (110 OPS+) with 23 doubles, seven triples, 12 home runs, 77 RBI, 91 runs and 42 steals. There's little doubt that PCA's 2026 season dwarfed this one overall, and Davis was far behind Mays (11.0) for the league lead in WAR.

For the rest of his career, Davis averaged 3.1 WAR per season, and though he had good years, he never reached 6.0 WAR again. The WAR figure was, again, mostly driven by defense. He had several good offensive seasons, but his only 20-homer season came in 1962 when he was 22, two years prior to his career year.

Davis' career probably looks a lot like PCA's apparent upside before his home run barrage in the first half of 2025. He racked up over 60 career WAR with a decent batting average, excellent defense and excellent baserunning.

With PCA reaching 30-30 last year and 40-40 this year, though, the bar has been raised.

César Cedeño followed up his 8.0 WAR season with a 7.4 season at age 22 and 5.8 at age 23. He was very good through age 29 and, in fact, the most statistically similar player through both ages 27 and 28 was Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski. Things fell apart after that. As a quick and easy way to illustrate it, Cedeño amassed 49.4 WAR through his age-29 season and only 3.6 in his final six years.

It's easier to remember that Andruw Jones' career unfolded in similar fashion because we witnessed it not too long ago and then discussed his Hall of Fame candidacy during his nine turns on the ballot before he finally made it in. In Jones' 12 Braves' season, he racked up 368 home runs, 1,117 RBI and 61 WAR while generally being considered the best defensive center fielder in baseball. Once he left, in time for his age-31 season, Jones accrued just 1.7 WAR in his last five seasons.

Through Jones' age-28 season, the most statistically similar players are Bryce Harper and Frank Robinson.

To compare these two to Crow-Armstrong, the argument would be that he'll continue to look like one of the best players in baseball -- even if taking steps backward from being the very best in the 2026 regular season -- before falling apart once he's around 30 years old.

Certainly possible, but given the adjustments he's already not only been willing to make at the plate, but eager to make, I'm just not seeing him all of a sudden hitting a wall. Sure, at some point he'll start losing speed and that'll affect his defensive range and baserunning, but why would the plate skills deteriorate all of a sudden?

Then again, few saw it coming with Jones.

All three of these players were on the path to having an argument as the best player in history before injuries derailed them in their 30s and left them as mere "all-time greats."

Through Mickey Mantle's age-30 season, he had 90.7 WAR. He averaged 121 games per year in his final six seasons, putting up 19.5 WAR. Through  Ken Griffey Jr.'s age-30 season, he had 76.2 WAR. He played 10 more seasons, but only amassed 7.6 more WAR. Through Mike Trout's age-27 season, he had 72.1 WAR (his top statistical similars were Mantle, Robinson and Griffey). We'll skip 2020 for obvious reasons, but since then he's averaged 90 games and 3.0 WAR per season.

Even with the drop-offs, it would be surprising to see Crow-Armstrong reach this level because it's surprising to see any player reach this lofty standard. In career WAR among center fielders, Mantle is fourth, Trout is fifth and Griffey is sixth. They trail only Cobb, Speaker and the guy we're going to discuss next. Joe DiMaggio is seventh.

Despite the lofty standard PCA set for himself in 2026, coming close to Willie Mays' career would be jaw-droppingly shocking, and that is absolutely not intended as a slight.

Mays has an argument as the greatest player in baseball history and he put himself in that discussion by being good at everything and doing it all with great longevity. From his age-23 to -35 seasons, he led the majors in WAR eight times, leading the NL an additional two times. His worst seasons in that timeframe were 7.6 and 7.8 WAR. In that span, he also led the league in runs twice, hits once, triples three times, home runs three times, stolen bases four times, average once, on-base percentage once, slugging percentage five times and OPS five times.

Mays even posted 5.2 WAR at age 39 and 6.3 at age 40. He led the NL with a .425 OBP when he was 40 years old! He hit .345/.411/.667 at age 23.

Mays' 156.2 career WAR ranks third among position players all-time behind two guys you might have heard of: Barry Bonds (162.8) and Babe Ruth (162.3).

I feel pretty strongly Pete Crow-Armstrong isn't headed for a run at this career and that's just fine.

The realistic long-term range for the 2026 National League MVP seems somewhere between Cedeño and Mantle. It's a wide variance of outcomes between those two, obviously, as well it should be when the player we discuss is only 24 years old. For his name to be mentioned among these at all is a testament to the year Crow-Armstrong just put together.

#2684. Former All-Star has created NBA’s biggest ‘f–king mess’ — and it just keeps getting worse

Situations don't get much uglier than Dejounte Murray's in New Orleans.

The Pelicans guard wants a trade from the franchise, and his relationship with the organization appears beyond repair.

But worst of all, opposing teams reportedly aren't biting, asking for draft compensation just to take him off New Orleans' hands in a trade.

"What a f–king mess," one NBA executive told Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko this week. "No one wants to touch him."

Dejounte Murray #5 of the New Orleans Pelicans reacts to a call during a game against the Denver Nuggets in New Orleans, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Getty Images

It's a quick fall for the former All-Star, whom the Pelicans acquired from the Hawks in a 2024 blockbuster deal for a package that included Dyson Daniels and two first-round picks.

Now, just over two years later, the Pelicans could be forced to give up even more assets to get rid of him.

Two opposing team officials told Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix they would demand a first-round pick to take on Murray's contract, which pays him $32.8 million this season and includes a $30.8 million player option for 2027-28.

Murray, 30, has appeared in just 54 games since arriving in New Orleans, having suffered a broken hand and a torn Achilles.

Dejounte Murray of the New Orleans Pelicans reacts during a game against the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

He's averaging 13.4 points and 4.4 assists through nine games this season, shooting just 29.6 percent from beyond the arc.

But his struggles on the court are only part of the problem.

Murray took to social media to lash out at critics earlier this month, suggesting someone within the organization was responsible for negative posts about him.

Dejounte Murray of the New Orleans Pelicans handles the ball against the LA Clippers on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif. NBAE via Getty Images

"The sabotage is real!" he wrote in a since-deleted post.

In another since-deleted tirade, Murray went after a Pelicans fan account that highlighted his mistakes during a blowout loss to the Nets.

"You have no f–king clue what we dealing with," Murray, who hasn't played since Nov. 11, wrote on the platform.

ESPN's Brian Windhorst subsequently claimed the Pelicans had sent Murray home following his trade request, while suggesting the guard had become difficult to keep around the team.

"They sent him home," Windhorst said on "The Hoop Collective" podcast.

"NEVER WAS SENT HOME," he wrote in the comments of a Bleacher Report Instagram post.

Murray has reportedly expressed interest in joining the Suns, with Phoenix guard Jalen Green floated as a potential trade piece.

But according to The Athletic's Sam Amick on Friday, recent discussions between the two teams lasted approximately five minutes and gained "zero traction."

The Suns reportedly don't want to take on Murray's contract without getting back draft compensation.

Iko added that Murray's unhappiness dates back to last season and was exacerbated by the Pelicans' drafting of young point guard Jeremiah Fears in 2025.

While the organization is seemingly ready to move forward without him, Murray could find himself stuck in New Orleans for the foreseeable future.

#2683. On this date: Packers lose to Colts in weird and wild game

There's no Packers game today, but that gives us plenty of time to crack open the history books and find some weirdness. We don't have to look too far, either. On this date in 2020, the Packers found themselves on the wrong end of a high-flying game in Indianapolis.

The Packers rolled into Indianapolis at 7-2 but in a bit of an inconsistent funk. They'd come out of their Week 5 bye flat against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and got slapped around, losing 38-10 in a grim foreshadowing of how their season would end. They beat the Texans, but fell to the Vikings at home 28-20 in an odd, wind-shortened game that saw both teams split a grand total of 15 possessions including a single-play kneeldown drive to end the first half. Then they'd handled the San Francisco 49ers, but struggled with the Jacksonville Jaguars. All in all, it was a confusing five-game stretch.

It wouldn't get better against the Colts.

The Packers turned the ball over twice in the first quarter, but the defense held off Philip Rivers (in his first Colts stint) and the Indianapolis offense long enough for Aaron Rodgers and company to find their feet in the second quarter. They reeled off three straight touchdown drives to take a 28-14 lead into halftime.

But true to form for that year, the offense bogged down in the third quarter. They went three and out twice in their only two third quarter possessions. Then, after return man Darrius Shepherd fumbled on a kickoff return early in the fourth quarter, the Packers would go on to turn the ball over on downs on their first drive of the final period.

All of that opened the door for a Colts rally. They scored three field goals and a touchdown on four straight second-half drives to take a 31-28 lead early in the fourth quarter. And then things got really weird.

Taking possession with just over eight minutes to go, the Packers navigated their way to the Colts' 34-yard line, but decided not to play for a tie when facing a 4th-and-1 play. But Aaron Rodgers' pass to Jamaal Williams fell incomplete, and the Colts had a golden opportunity to put the game away.

But as is so often the case, the men in stripes had different thoughts.

The Colts were flagged five times on their ensuing drive, including four holding penalties and one for illegal motion. But lest you think the refs were being one sided, the Packers were also flagged twice on the same drive, once when Preston Smith jumped offside and then, bizarrely, for having too many men on the field after the dead ball caused by Smith's offside. At one point, there were penalties on one team or the other on five straight plays.

Eventually, the Colts' drive bogged down and the Packers took over for one last, desperate drive on beginning on their own six-yard line. Rodgers threw incomplete on first and second down, but facing a 3rd and 10 with just over a minute to go, he launched a moon shot to Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who somehow hauled it in for a 47-yard gain. Back in business, the Packers managed to get all the way to the Colts' eight-yard line but couldn't find the end zone. Mason Crosby converted a 26-yard field goal to tie the game, though, and the contest headed for overtime.

The Packers won the toss, but it didn't take long for everything to come undone. After a completion to Aaron Jones on first down, Marquez Valdes-Scantling fumbled a short pass, turning the ball over deep in Packers' territory. Four plays later, the game was over.

Valdes-Scantling's fumble prompted a pointed, if a bit overly dramatic, question. "How can you live with Marquez Valdes-Scantling?" asked a beat writer of Matt LaFleur. The question did little but reflect fan outrage after the costly mistake, and make no mistake, fans were incensed. MVS reported receiving death threats after his costly mistake, which is a curious reaction considering the Packers wouldn't have even made it to overtime had he not been the one responsible for a high-difficulty catch near the end of regulation.

But nobody ever claimed being a sports fan is logical. And after a game as odd and disjointed as the one they witnessed that November day, you can at least understand why fans may have come out of it feeling a bit raw.

Still, don't threaten players. That's too far.

#2682. Updated Big Ten football standings, title game scenarios, bowl tracker

The Big Ten sprinkled in a bit of chaos in Week 12 with its top two teams in the rankings and the Big Ten standings each leaving the door cracked for a wild Big Ten championship game race in the final weekend of the regular season. Losses by UCLA and Indiana means there are still two spots in the Big Ten championship game to fill going into the final weekend of the regular season, and there is still hope for Iowa and Oregon.

Meanwhile, Penn State's shocking loss at home to Rutgers means the Nittany Lions will finish below .500 in conference play this season.

Here are the updated Big Ten football standings following the results of Week 12.

UCLA and Indiana each missed out on clinching their spots in the Big Ten championshbip game with road losses in Week 12. That leaves the door open for Iowa and Oregon heading into the final weekend of the Big Ten regular season.

Here are the Big Ten championship game clinching scenarios in play heading into Week 13. It's a bit more complicated than it could have been.

OR UCLA loses AND Iowa wins AND Wisconsin wins

OR UCLA loses AND Indiana wins AND Minnesota wins

AND Wisconsin beats Minnesota, USC beats UCLA, AND Oregon beats Washington

OR UCLA beats USC AND Washignton beats Oregon

OR UCLA loses AND Oregon wins AND Minnesota beats Wisconsin

There will be no bowl eligibility drama on the final weekend of Big Ten regular season play. The Big Ten has seen all but teams clinch bowl eligibility for the 2026 season, while the other four will be unable to meet the win minimum for postseason play this season. The only exception would be Maryland as a 5-win team if bowl spots open up and Maryland is eligible for consideration (if Maryland wins against Penn State in Week 13).

All that is left to determine is how many Big Ten teams will reach the College Football Playoff and which bowl games the other bowl-eligible teams will be invited to.

ELIGIBLE (6+ wins): Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Northwestern, Ohio State, Oregon, Penn State, UCLA, USC, Washington, Wisconsin

INELIGIBLE (7+ losses): Maryland, Michigan State, Purdue, Rutgers

If you were wondering, and I was, the NHL record for longest winless streak to start a season is 15 in a row by the 1943-44 New York Rangers. They lost 11 straight, tied a game, then lost three more before knocking off the visiting Boston Bruins.

So the Kings (0-4-2) have a long way to get there and haven't even tied the franchise record yet, as the 1984-85 club was winless in its first nine. L.A. still made the playoffs that year. This year's club is still priced +100 for extra hockey with No only slightly favored at -125. The updated season points total is 90.5 – remember, 84 regular-season games now. The Kings' preseason points total was 95.5, so the sportsbooks haven't given up on them yet, nor should they. Still too talented of a roster.

The goaltending has been problem No. 1, with the duo of Darcy Kuemper and Anton Forsberg combining for a 4.17 goals-against average that is third-worst in the NHL and an .861 save percentage that is second-to-last. The penalty kill ranks 31st at 61.9%. Perhaps a trade for Winnipeg holdout Connor Hellebuyck?

But the offense needs help too, putting up just 2.00 goals per game (31st) and converting 14.3% of the time on the power play (26th). L.A. scored eight total goals in its first two games and has scored exactly one in the next four. That's hard to do.

Injuries haven't helped, with the likes of Kevin Fiala, Alex Turcotte and Mats Zuccarello all on injured reserve. Coach Peter Laviolette said that Zuccarello is "trending" toward playing tonight, however, after practicing Monday on a line with center Quinton Byfield and Trevor Moore. No one has more than five points, and only three guys have a positive rating (all at plus-1).

"I'm not seeing [the lapses] from our fourth-line type players, I'm seeing it from our top players," All-Star defenseman and team captain Drew Doughty said over the weekend. "That's why we're losing games. Your top players need to be your best players every night and not just have flashes of brilliance. They need to play 60 minutes."

We should note that the Kings started 1-3-2 last season ahead of a long trip as similar to starts tonight, and they still managed to sneak into the playoffs, although they were then swept by Colorado. But I sure don't see any sure-fire wins on this five-game roadie. It likely will be Kuemper tonight, and in two road starts he has allowed 10 goals on 61 shots.

#2679. Film Review: Miami Hurricanes 28 – Virginia Tech Hokies 20

The Miami Hurricanes (10-1) knocked off the Virginia Tech Hokies (6-5) after starting the game down 14-0. Miami slowly chipped away at the Hokies lead until overtaking them with a pair of 4th quarter TD's.

The Canyonero Keys to Victory main theme for the game was to keep their head down and drive. The 'Canes decided that was an option in the 2nd quarter where Miami scored 11 points to bring the within three at the half.

The individual keys to victory over VT for Miami were:

1- Contain Overton better than Sheppard. Jeffrey Overton averaged only 2.9 yards per carry against Miami while only scoring once on a short TD pass. He was not as effective as Sheppard from Duke and that helped Miami stay in this one until it took the lead.

2- Play that deep 1/3 country cover 3. I was wrong about this one. Miami went to man and it flipped the script in the 2nd half. The 'Canes locked the Hokies up and gave them no room to dink and dunk.

3- Ground and pound 'em. Miami had a little spark from Darian Mensah's legs on scrambles, but the ground game was a plodding horse led by Fletchers' 63 yards and three TD's.

I predicted the 'Canes would win by 17, but no one could've assumed VT would jump to a 14 point lead off of an 8-minute drive and a short-field turnover.

On money downs, Miami took the advantage finishing 9-of-15 while Va. Tech finished 5-of-14. The 'Canes were struggling early on that opening drive before the defense put the clamps on the Hokies.

Miami lost the penalty battle as the 'Canes were flagged for 45 yards in penalties vs. VT's mere 10 yards.

The Hurricanes also lost the turnover margin battle having turned it over twice to VT's flawless game in that department.

Both kickers finished 2-for-2 on field goals. So if you look at the doppler this game should lean towards VT and not Miami, but the 'Canes won by eight… how?

This was by far Mensah's worst performance as a Hurricane. The Heisman Trophy candidate QB averaged only 6.5 yards per pass attempt with two INT's and failed to throw a TD pass. If you'd given me these stats pre-game I would've said there's no way Miami beats VT.

Both Mensah picks were in weird circumstances: the first being tipped off Javian Mallory's hands and the 2nd was on what the offense thought was a 'free play' from defensive offsides but wasn't flagged. Mensah had thrown it up there thinking he'd get a 2nd chance but it was picked off with no flag.

Mensah found eight different targets with only three averaging double-digit yards per catch marks. His clear favorite was Cooper Barkate who caught seven balls. VT had three PBU's against Miami.

The offensive line allowed two sacks and five TFL's along with pressures that Mensah scrambled out of or threw INC's.

Above- You have to come down with this ball. Is it high? Sure, but both hands got on the ball, that's a huge mistake from Mallory that becomes a tip drill INT.

Above- I think Pringle got called on wide sweep once for 12 yards and then boom it vanished like Keyser Söze. You can run this with a tunnel backside to Barkate, a 3rd level RPO post to him, too. I hope they don't shelve it.

Above- Fletcher's eyes on pass pro are off. He misses a lot of clear blocks he needs to make while trying to get out in the flat and on this one that led to a sack.

Above- Once you're beat inside as an OL your job is to just run block the guy (drive block) him and let the QB work off of you. OT is beat inside, TE is beat outside- creates a seam for Mensah and he runs for the 1st down. Really heads up play by him to escape.

Above- Things that Upshaw is good at: coming open on four verts and Y Cross when he's the 'over' route guy. Keep letting him be this guy on Y-Cross.

Above- If you're going to throw this ball it has to be where Mensah dropped the time, high and outside. Back pylon throws are high and away, front pylon throws are low and away.

Above- Things Upshaw shouldn't be doing are serving as a key blocker on a screen. He's terrible at it and reminds me of Jacolby George when Dawson tried the same thing with him. Use people in their strengths, mask their weaknesses.

Above- I get that you've thrown a pick at this point but either fire this one to the dude open deep or check down short. Don't take a sack to avoid a 2nd INT re the deep throw.

Above- one of the strange parts of this did he didn't he jump thing was Barkate not giving full effort. He gets the ball snatched away and then doesn't play through the whistle. Let the refs figure it out later, you have to treat it like a live play. A to B + 2 steps.

Above- I love slide routes off play-action to any and everyone. This is a winged WR coming across the formation. Close and far TE's, RB's out of the backfield. These routes are so hard to defend look at that space he has!

Above- Fletcher is banged up but he has enough gas in the tank when he needs to. He left the Hokies spread out and diving for grass like he threw a grenade at them.

The defense started off slowly, allowing a 15 play, 75 yard, 8-minute drive for a touchdown on VT's opening series. They followed that up with a one play, 15 yards TD scoring drive off the interception. What many forget is that was only two plays of rest after a drive that surpassed the typical drive by 10 plays and 5 minutes. That's a tall ask after that opening score and only a 41-second drive from the offense.

Ethan Grunkemeyer averaged 4.8 yards per pass attempt with one TD and was ineffective in any run game for the Hokies. The Hokies hit only six different receivers with only Que'Sean Brown going off. Brown averaged 13.4 yards per catch on seven receptions. Miami squashed the big play and kept Reynolds from busting out.

Overton was held to 2.7 yards per carry on 14 touches while Messiah Mickens had the one 15 yard carry and then just a two yard rush. The Miami defense logged two sacks, two PBU's and six TFL's led by Ahmad Moten's pair of TFL's.

Xavier Lucas had a sack and 1.5 TFL's, Justin Scott had another "David Blay Award" moment with an encroachment, and Damon Wilson recorded his first sack since October 3rd. Ah early October, the weather was still warm as was Dabo Swinney's hot seat.

Above- Back to head down, eyes down and lunging at ball carriers. That opening drive was painful to watch.

Above- Day left his feet but holds on long enough for help to arrive. That's what you need against a big strong TE like VT's. Just hold on and rally to the tackle.

Above- I too would get Dunnigan in a 1-on-1 with my RB. The back uses an inside-out move and gets a step on the young safety. TD Hokies. I was concerned at this point. That was a hell of a drive but sometimes scripted drives are like that.

Above- So he comes down on the 2-way-go (I think this is Day). But he doesn't buzz his feet. He then lowers his head and lunges to leave his feet. All no-no's of making a tackle. This is the 15-yard TD to go up 14-0.

Above- Maybe Hetherman has learned a little lesson and brought pressure from Lucas at 4y away vs. 15y away. Lucas gets home and it's a sack and a punt.

Above- Later Lucas lets the WR get even and when they're even they're leavin'. You have the depth on him, keep it. Don't get in a foot race with a guy that knows where the ball is going.

Above- Moten starts to cook late in this one. Here he's unblockable on a TFL. His first step was so quick they couldn't even hold him.

Above- Beat off the edge right away, Miami gets another sack. Nice to see Wilson on the stat sheet. He celebrated his sack like he won the Super Bowl.

Above- How do you take a game back over and squeeze the life out of it? Interior DL play. When DT's are great the game is impossible for an OC. QB's hate pressure in their face, the run game hates mesh charges and interior pressure vs zone.

Miami has survived quite a few scares this season, making me think back to 2024 but even more so to 2017. Mensah is a better QB than Malik Rosier (not a stab at Rosier, just the truth) and Mario Cristobal has improved his coaching chops since '24, even if only slightly.

One thing you can say is that the last three years of the Cristobal Era have shown this isn't a program that accepts quitting. Cal and VT in '24, Indiana in '25, and now UNC, FSU, VT, Duke, ND… people are throwing the kitchen sink at Miami and the 'Canes are fighting til the end.

Miami has now qualified for only the 'Canes second ACC Championship Game trip, and 3rd overall qualification (self imposed ban removed Miami from one trip to Charlotte) since joining the ACC. That's a sad stat but in the final year of the ACCCG the lads are heading to Charlotte!

#2678. NHL Power Rankings: Bruins, Jeremy Swayman off to a roaring start in a tough Atlantic Division

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

You can't make the playoffs in 10 games, but you can definitely give yourself some breathing room when the inevitable ebbs and flows of the season strike. That's exactly what the Boston Bruins have done as they've stood out for the right reasons in a deep Atlantic Division.

Boston currently leads the division with 15 points, and while the Tampa Bay Lightning's record is technically better, the Bruins' plus-14 goal differential is tied for second in the NHL.

The biggest reason for this fast start has been the play of Jeremy Swayman in goal. He's allowed one or fewer goals in half of his starts, and Swayman's 8.02 goals saved above average ranks second to old Beantown running mate Linus Ullmark, per Natural Stat Trick.

We have a long way to go before we start discussing Vezina Trophy candidates seriously, but Swayman certainly has the potential to carry Boston to the postseason.

It helps that David Pastrnak is an elite playmaker, and the Bruins have been getting contributions from young forwards Fraser Minten and James Hagens. Morgan Geekie has also gone from goal-scoring machine to distributor with seven assists in 10 games.

The Atlantic Division will be a heavyweight brawl throughout the season, but to this point, the Bruins have proven to be a worthy combatant. With that in mind, here are the updated NHL Power Rankings.

#2677. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Celtics win Jaylen Brown trade (for now), Trae Young looks done

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every now and then, the NBA gives us a week that is essentially built around a single game. A total of 51 games were played in the last week, but come on, the one you remember was Jaylen Brown's long-awaited reunion with Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers squared off in a battle of the Eastern Conference's two top seeds on Tuesday, and even if the game fell short of our basketball expectations, it provided more than enough beef to sate us. Brown snubbed Tatum before the game. Paul George gave a fan the middle finger. Appropriate animosity has returned to this eternal rivalry.

So... how did we handle that from a winners and losers perspective? Well, Boston is an obvious winner, but Brown escaped loser status. It's winners and losers of the week. Philly won its two other games this week, and Brown led all scorers in Sunday's win with 31 points. He certainly lost on Tuesday. He may yet wind up losing the trade. But we're not docking him a whole week for a single poor performance. So if Brown escaped the loser's section, who made it? And who joins Boston in the winner's circle? Let's look back at the week that was.

Boston's big win over Philadelphia underlined something that's been evident all season: Paul George, at least thus far, has been better as a Celtic than Jaylen Brown has been as a 76er. There are obviously circumstantial reasons for that. George is at his best as a force-multiplier, and he's on a team on which he doesn't need to play an enormous role. Brown is at his best as a floor-raiser, but he's on a team full of floor-raisers. That doesn't mean Philadelphia regrets the trade -- it got them LeBron James! -- but it does suggest that, after months of criticism, the Celtics at least got what they were looking for out of the deal.

Everything the Celtics were good at a year ago, they're still good at. They were one of the NBA's best shooting teams last season, and George both makes more 3s than Brown and takes far more of them. They were great at protecting the basket last season and George's activity as a helper has been a net benefit to their rim-protection.

Yet George's presence has also been the catalyst for improvement in a few other key areas. Boston never generated turnovers defensively last season and they do this year, in part because George is averaging the sixth-most steals and third-most deflections in the NBA. They're getting to the line at a roughly league-average rate, in part because the ball doesn't stick to George as it so often did Brown. It's easier to get defenses in rotation with the ball moving and 3-pointers flying. Tatum has benefited enormously in this respect with a career-best 46% free-throw rate.

Again, the 76ers are perfectly happy with their end of the deal. They traded old for young. They got James on the minimum. They're 11-3. But Boston emerged with the player who has made a bigger difference thus far this season, and it got two first-round draft assets in the process. That doesn't mean the Celtics necessarily win the trade in the long run, but it does suggest, unsurprisingly, that Brad Stevens understood his own team and what it needed better than the rest of us.

Well, they haven't lost in three weeks... so this feels overdue. Let's talk about the much ballyhooed three-guard lineup for a moment. The Spurs couldn't keep bringing Dylan Harper off the bench this season. He's simply too good and too important to their future to risk alienating. They couldn't bench De'Aaron Fox immediately either. Former All-Stars tend to take such decisions as a sign of disrespect, and such a move could have splintered the locker room.

So the Spurs made the somewhat awkward decision to start the three of them together. The season's second game, a loss to the Houston Rockets, showcased exactly why so many feared the fit of the three of them together. Three iffy guard-sized shooters minimized spacing for the sake of redundant ball-handling, and the Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle trio got outscored by 12 points in a four-point defeat. Well, the three guards haven't lost their minutes together in a single game since then. They're +112 in 115 minutes after that point.

Now, there are notable caveats here. Every three-man combination of Spurs that has played at least 100 minutes since then is firmly positive, and the three guards have literally not played a single minute together this season that did not come alongside Victor Wembanyama. It's entirely possible that Wembanyama is so game-breaking that any lineup he's a part of is an almost automatic winner. But that would work in favor of the three guards here. Maybe San Antonio is so much more talented than the field that it can afford to play suboptimal lineups for the sake of maintaining harmony in the locker room.

That may prove more challenging late in a playoff series, but it's easier to convince players to change their roles for, say, Game 5 of the Western Conference Finals than it is in November or December. The Spurs might have to think harder about this in a field that included a healthy Oklahoma City, but with the Thunder compromised, San Antonio is such a large favorite to win the Western Conference that it can afford to try to just out-talent everyone else. So far, it's clearly working.

We are in all-out panic mode over the state of Cleveland's starting lineup. James Harden can't get to the rim anymore. Donovan Mitchell just signed a supermax extension that already feels iffy. Peyton Watson's shooting has fallen off a cliff and he's struggling as a primary point-of-attack defender. The Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen partnership is getting crushed in its joint minutes. The starters have played 99 minutes together and lost those minutes by 24 points. No five-man unit that has played that many minutes has been outscored by more. Malaise doesn't do this core justice. Clearly, something here has to change.

Fortunately, there appear to be some internal solutions here. After FAA issues forced the Cavaliers to spend Friday night in Miami, Mitchell called for Saturday's game against the Dallas Mavericks to be postponed. The Cavaliers didn't arrive in Dallas until around noon on Saturday. The starters sat out. Cleveland won the game by 10 against a healthy, playoff-caliber opponent. Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson all scored between 18 and 24 points.

This wasn't a one-off. Thomas is outscoring Harden and Mobley on a per-minute basis. Proctor is sporting a better-than-6-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio on the season, and Synergy Sports rates him in the 100th percentile on spot-up efficiency and the 96th in pick-and-rolls, including passes, in terms of points per possession. Tyson breathes life into a transition offense that is otherwise a sore spot. Most of this team's energy comes from the bench.

What exactly the solution here is, we can't say. It will involve a trade. Perhaps a few. But there's something here, and the early indications are that things are going to get better for the team as a whole when it eventually starts leaning on these players a bit more.

Dejounte Murray requested a trade this week. That's not a rumor. The Pelicans publicly acknowledged it and Murray retweeted the news from ESPN. Meanwhile, after Monday's loss to the Golden State Warriors, Jordan Poole was asked if he would ever come back to the team with which he started his career. He answered "yes." Players tend to not be that definitive in those statements, nor do they tend to acknowledge that their former team "just feels like home." It certainly seems as though there's somewhere he'd rather be than New Orleans.

To borrow a phrase from social media user Nathan Calvin, "if you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." Essentially... if two players seem this eager to flee, more probably do as well. Sam Amick suggested in a radio interview over the summer that Trey Murphy would like to play elsewhere. There has been plenty of speculation about other Pelicans as well. A 4-10 start following 26- and 21-win seasons tends to do that.

We're more than a year into Joe Dumars' reign as head of basketball operations and there's no discernible plan here. Virtually every key player from last year's roster was retained and the team has largely been healthier than it was a year ago, but they're on pace for a worse record under new head coach Jamahl Mosley. The sad thing is that the Pelicans have a fair number of valuable players. They've just assembled those players so carelessly that they've become far less than the sum of their parts. This team is incoherent, and even the players seem to know it.

Trae Young was held scoreless in 26 minutes on Sunday. It was the first time he's been held scoreless in his entire NBA career, but it may be the final straw of a trend that has been bubbling for some time: Trae Young is simply no longer a star-level scorer. He currently has his lowest shooting percentage from both 2-point and 3-point range in a single season. He lacks the burst to get to the rim or beat mismatches consistently anymore, and he's never developed comfort as a catch-and-shooter. Aside from free throws, it's basically all jumpers off the dribble and floaters, neither of which he's making at the rate he needs to in order to justify his defensive shortcomings. He scored 37 points against Detroit last Monday, but needed 17 free throws to get there on less than 35% shooting from the floor. He needs whistles right now.

This is a version of Young who probably shouldn't monopolize an offense, yet he's never shown that he's capable of playing differently. The Wizards are spending 26 possessions a game on shots Young generates either for himself or a teammate out of pick-and-roll, more than any other player in the league, per Synergy Sports. As of Sunday, he and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were tied for the league lead among starters in average seconds possessing the ball per touch, per NBA.com tracking data. The younger players who represent the future of this organization are spending a whole lot of time watching someone else dribble. Nobody is really spacing the floor for anyone else since there's so little shooting on this roster. The Wizards have played close to neutral when Young rests, but are getting outscored by more than 10 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor. That difference is almost entirely offensive, yet Young remains the same defensive liability he's always been.

This is where the four-year max contract Washington bewilderingly gave Young becomes so destructive. The basic notion of acquiring a high-end point guard to serve as an offensive organizer for these young wings made sense on paper, but they committed to him essentially sight unseen. He played five mostly meaningless games in a tanking season and they paid him max money without really knowing how he'd fit with the team they were building. If he'd walked for nothing in free agency, well, it's not as though they spent picks to get him. Now they're stuck paying star-level money for a non-star-level player who probably can't meaningfully scale down his involvement in the offense because he just doesn't provide much value when any other player on either team has the basketball.

There are a lot of things going wrong in Washington right now, but Young is inevitably going to be the face of those struggles because he's the player the Wizards just bewilderingly gave a four-year max contract to in order to re-sign. Jaylen Brown had the loudest individual loss of the week, but he at least won all of his other games and has largely been what his team has asked him to be. Young went winless this week, had a scoreless game, and maintained his mostly disappointing season-long performance.

If you would have heard "the Warriors have a -2.4 net rating a month into the 2026-27 season," you probably would have shrugged and said, "sure, sounds about right." The Warriors were widely pegged as a low-end Play-In, high-end lottery team before the season, and a -2.4 net rating projects out to a win total in the 30s. Except that isn't Golden State's net rating. It's Golden State's net rating in the minutes Stephen Curry has missed this season.

That's how far above expectations Golden State was playing during its eight-game winning streak. The Curry-off version of the team was around average; the Curry-on version of the team was a juggernaut. The latter feels a bit unsustainable, but we won't know again for around a month. The former is what's about to be tested now that Curry has an oblique abdominal tear. The Spurs hardly represent a fair test for a team in this situation, but San Antonio predictably waxed Golden State by 38 in the first game of Curry's absence.

Nobody's asking for another eight-game winning streak. Those wins are banked, and Golden State's season begins in earnest when Jimmy Butler returns in January or February. For now, the Warriors just need to stay afloat. Find wins where the schedule offers them, and fortunately, the Pelicans, Kings, Clippers and Jazz are on the docket in the next three weeks or so. But losing Curry is a reminder of how fragile that streak really was. Maybe, now that Yaxel Lendeborg is emerging as a possible star, the Warriors are capable of genuine postseason success this season. But the health of any 38-year-old not named LeBron James is going to be precarious. Things could be a lot worse, but Curry's injury drags one of the feel-good stories of the early season back down to Earth.

#2675. MLB rumors: Rangers in mix for Sato, Dodgers seek infield help, Korean slugger could join free agent class

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with only one significant transaction: Evan Phillips signed with the Braves. Phillips, our 34th-ranked free agent, received a three-year deal worth $35 million. He'll replace Raisel Iglesias in Atlanta's bullpen and pair with Robert Suarez at the end of the game. The Braves could still re-sign Iglesias too, I suppose.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors -- A LOT of rumors -- and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The Rangers are among the teams with interest in Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports The Athletic. Sato primarily played third base for the Hanshin Tigers, though he does not stand out defensively, and could land at first base or in the corner outfield in MLB. Texas could stand to upgrade at first base and could always slot Sato in at DH as well.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available and the best free agent position player. The reigning Triple Crown winner in Japan hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. Sato, 28 in March, has some similarities to Munetaka Murakami as a lefty with big power and swing-and-miss concerns, though Sato is a much more aggressive hitter and won't walk as much as Murakami.

With Miguel Rojas retired, the Dodgers are looking to add a right-handed hitting infielder, according to The Athletic. Mookie Betts and Max Muncy are entrenched on the left side of the infield. Tommy Edman, a switch-hitter, is penciled in at second base, with fellow switch-hitter Alex Freeland next in line as depth. Freeland has not hit much in his limited MLB time, however.

This is not a great free agent class overall, but it does feature several utility infielders who hit right-handed. Among them are Mauricio Dubón, Ha-Seong Kim, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Edmundo Sosa. Glovemen Oswald Peraza (Angels) and Jared Triolo (Pirates) are potential trade targets. Rojas was a very productive role player for Los Angeles. He won't be so easy to replace.

The Padres are receiving calls about catchers Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Top prospect Ethan Salas was called up in September and became the youngest catcher to appear in the postseason in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. Salas is the future behind the plate, making Campusano or Fermin (or perhaps both) expendable.

Campusano and Fermin are very different players. Campusano is a bat-first catcher who might be worth keeping given his age (28) and the fact that the Padres could slot him at DH. That said, those same qualities make him appealing to other teams. Fermin, 31, is a terrific defender who hasn't hit much the last few years. The Padres need pitching and could deal a catcher or two for an arm or two.

Samsung Lions outfielder Ja-Wook Koo has hired a new agent and is looking to make the jump to MLB, reports MLB.com. Koo, a 10-time All-Star and this year's Korean Series MVP, has been among the best hitters in the Korea Baseball Organization the last few years. The 33-year-old hit .371/.458/.581 with 15 homers and nearly as many walks (66) as strikeouts (71) in 2026.

Koo's age and the fact he's a left-handed hitter in a market inundated with left-handed hitting outfielders will work against him in free agency. He has a great track record in Korea, though, including a history of high contact rates, which could make him a cheaper and more appealing target than MLB free agents like Michael Conforto, Trent Grisham, Cedric Mullins, and Daulton Varsho.

#2674. Tari Eason gives amazing, blunt explanation for his 25-point game: 'S--t, the Wizards, for real'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Rockets improved to 11-3 on the season with a 147-119 beatdown of the Washington Wizards on Sunday night.

While Houston is no stranger to an offensive explosion, ranking second in the NBA this season in offensive rating (121.2), the 147 points scored on Sunday were 12 more than they've scored in a game this season. It was a balanced scoring effort as a team, as six players reached double figures and three scored at least 25 points -- including Tari Eason off the bench.

That 25-point performance represents a new season high for Eason -- his previous best was a 19-point effort against the Hawks -- as he went 10 for 14 from the field and 3 of 5 from 3-point range in 30 minutes off the bench. That effort earned Eason the honor of the walk-off TV interview, during which he gave a brutally honest (and hilarious) answer for why he was able to set a new season high and do so efficiently.

"Shit, the Wizards, for real. It was them," Eason said.

Tari Eason on what allowed him to have a season-high 25 points off the bench tonight:"Shit, the Wizards, for real." pic.twitter.com/t4bOwtzw5r

A+ work here, no notes. Eason could've puffed out his chest after beating up on the Wizards or complimented his teammates for allowing him to get in a rhythm, but instead chose the honest route rarely taken by players in a post-game interview and simply admitted that anyone could get buckets on Washington.

The Wizards are not the worst defense in the NBA -- that honor belongs to the Chicago Bulls -- but they are 25th in defensive rating and certainly do not boast very many elite defenders. Clearly, Eason didn't feel like he was doing anything special or out of the ordinary on Sunday night on his way to 25 points off the bench, and gave credit where it was due to the other team.

Unfortunately for the Wizards, it is not credit they'd like to take, and this feels like the kind of (earned) disrespect that should light some kind of fire under Washington.

#2673. Could Tarik Skubal take a short-term, high-AAV contract? Breaking down pros and cons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The expectation is left-hander and two-time AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent available this offseason, will sign a record contract before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are almost certain to lock out the players at that time. Skubal is expected to sign before then.

Skubal, 30 later this month, is a Scott Boras client and Boras tends to shatter records, not beat them narrowly. There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:

Something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

With that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a new contract to stay with his team.

1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a new salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the big picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.
