#2639. Patriots WR A.J. Brown expected to miss multiple weeks due to hamstring injury, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The injuries for the New England Patriots continue to pile up. Wide receiver A.J. Brown is expected to miss multiple weeks with a hamstring injury, per reports. The news comes the same day as reports that quarterback Drake Maye is expected to miss most, if not all, of the remainder of the regular season with a broken right fibula.

Brown suffered the hamstring injury during their Week 10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany. The 29-year-old has dealt with numerous injuries this season, finding himself on the injury report more times than not.

The three-time Pro Bowler suffered an ankle injury in their season opener and was placed on injured reserve, missing four games. After he returned, he then missed two games due to a knee strain.

What started as a slew of hopeful possibilities for the Patriots, with Brown and Maye leading the offense, has dipped quite dramatically. The duo has played together in just four games this season, and in those four games, Brown has 11 receptions for 128 yards and no touchdowns.

The Patriots are currently on a bye, but even with the extra time to rest, Brown is expected to be sidelined for multiple games.

The wide receiver room now consists of Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism and Kyle Williams. Romeo Doubs will be eligible to return from IR when the team returns from its bye week.

The Patriots acquired Brown this offseason from the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 first-round pick.

New England currently sits at 5-5 and will face the Los Angeles Chargers when it returns from the bye in Week 12.

#2638. Which team needs Tarik Skubal the most? Ranking the suitors for the best free agent available

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As we emerge from the recent General Manager Meetings and move toward the expected Dec. 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners, we might see an accelerated pace of activity soon. The most tantalizing possibility is that ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the undisputed top talent on the free agent market this winter, will sign before the sport shuts down for an indeterminate amount of time.

The decorated lefty, who soon turns 30, is our No. 1 free agent of the 2026-27 class, and it's not an especially close call. Here's part of our write-up:

"Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself."

Will he set the record for the biggest contract ever signed by a pitcher? Will Skubal fetch the highest average annual salary for a pitcher? Will he top $400 million? Those are all reasonable questions to ask. First, though, there's a question to be asked about the teams that are already pursuing him the most vigorously. That question is, which team needs him the most? We're restricting our discussion to the five teams that have been most reliably linked to Skubal so far this offseason. We're already hearing reports of surprise teams, and it's always possible a surprise late bidder will enter the fray and even win his signature, but for now, these five clubs are the favorites. This, then, is an ordering of those teams based on which desperately needs a talent like Skubal in order to reach their goals in 2027 and beyond. Let's get to it, in order from "needs him the most" to "needs him but not as urgently as the teams ahead of them" …

The Cubs are in contention mode and in need of roster improvements if they're going to run down the world champion Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central. The rotation is without question the most pressing need for Chicago. Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, David Peterson, and deadline acquisition Clay Holmes are all free agents. Justin Steele hasn't taken the mound at the big-league level since early in the 2025 season thanks to UCL surgery and a halting recovery process. While he's expected to be ready for 2027, he's not exactly a known quantity right now. Young upsider Cade Horton may not be back until midseason after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and Ben Brown, who recently had neck surgery, may be on a similar timeline. So, yes, the Cubs need a lot of rotation help, and Skubal would give them the true frontline ace they'd lack even if everyone were healthy. Unfortunately for the Cubs fans, it sounds like the Ricketts aren't willing to be truly competitive for his services.

Coming off the grave disappointments of 2026, the Mets could certainly use a headline-grabbing addition to improve their chances in 2027 and inspire a surely disaffected fan base. Beyond that, the Mets need more starting pitching to accompany promising young Nolan McLean. Christian Scott seems like a lock, but he doesn't project as a frontliner. They have some depth options for the back end, but they need a true needle-mover like Skubal at the very front. That's especially the case in what figures to be a hotly competitive NL East in 2027. Thus far, David Stearns and owner Steve Cohen sound committed to making a good-faith run at Skubal.

The Padres have a lot of work to do if they're going to earn a fourth straight playoff appearance. Speaking of which, the rotation is crying out for help right about now. They lost Dylan Cease to free agency last winter, and this time Michael King may be bound elsewhere, too. The Pads declined their club option on Nick Pivetta, and while they hope to bring him back on more favorable terms, there's no guarantee they'll be able to do that. Yes, Joe Musgrove will be back, but how much can he give them and how effective will he be? They'll need even more help if Adrian Morejon, a lockdown bulk reliever and possible starter-conversion project, signs elsewhere. Skubal's made to order, and signing the top talent on the market would be a strong signal by new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones that the team's recent tradition of spending and contending won't be fading away.

The Dodgers self-evidently needed Skubal enough to acquire him from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the deadline and do so at significant cost. On paper, the Dodgers aren't as desperate for rotation help as the teams ahead of them on this list, but there's still a need. Yoshinobu Yamamoto is a certifiable ace, but behind him Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are established health and durability risks. Shohei Ohtani is something of an unknown, at least insofar as his pitching is concerned right now, and thus far Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan have not proved worthy of being relied upon. One can squint and see the Dodgers' current championship window closing in the reasonably near future, which means that's all the more reason to push the chips in now. Retaining the elite services of Skubal would greatly aid the cause in 2027.

Eyeball a rotation that already includes Dylan Cease, José Soriano, and Trey Yesavage, and you might think it doesn't need much more. And maybe it doesn't. As a matter of principle, though, any team with contending aspirations should be interested in a top-shelf ace when he hits the market. The Jays, who in recent years have invested in the roster at commendable levels, are no doubt dreaming of a Skubal-Cease one-two punch that would be the envy of, oh, every other team in baseball. There's also depth to think about. In particular, Cody Ponce is a bit of an unknown coming off knee surgery that ended his 2026 season in the middle of his first start. Addressing the offense probably should be more of a priority for the Jays this winter, but, again, it's Tarik Skubal, and the likes of Tarik Skubal make any team better.

#2636. Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

The Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

Let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

There are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

This is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

He's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape shows an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

That brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

Most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

The theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

Part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

Mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

The paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

They could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

If Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

We're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

The Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

When the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

You can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The big swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

That, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

Speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

It's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

The Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

The Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.

#2635. Drake Maye out indefinitely with fibula: Big picture questions now facing Patriots offseason, beyond

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There are still seven games left on the schedule, but New England's season unofficially and unceremoniously ended in the aftermath of Week 10. That's due to Drake Maye suffering a broken fibula, which will sideline him deep into the regular season if not for the whole year. The Patriots' chances of returning to the playoffs after a surprise run to the Super Bowl a year ago are all but out the window.

The team enters its Week 11 bye at 5-5 and is slotted as the No. 8 seed in the conference. With Maye on the shelf and Tommy DeVito poised to start the rest of the way (unless they add a free agent), the second half could be tough sledding for Mike Vrabel's team. That's especially true in December, when they'll have a three-week stretch against the Bills, Vikings, and Chiefs. Even with Maye in the fold, those were going to be tough matchups to overcome. Without their star franchise quarterback, they're borderline insurmountable.

Really, this injury to Maye changes the lens through which we need to view the Patriots. The focus shifts away from the nitty-gritty of the regular season and possible playoff position to the bigger-picture, existential topics that extend beyond 2026. Below, we'll highlight some of the ripple effects of Maye's injury, along with other pressing questions facing the franchise as they look to bounce back in 2027 with their star QB in the fold.

One element of Maye's injury that is worth highlighting is that it comes at a less-than-ideal time for the quarterback, who becomes extension-eligible this offseason. It's hard to imagine this injury truly derailing any sort of negotiation between Maye's camp and the Patriots front office. That said, you can't really rule it out either.

That's especially true considering Maye could be—and should be—looking to reset the market at the position. After all, he already has an MVP runner-up and a Super Bowl appearance on his résumé. That means exceeding Patrick Mahomes' $64 million-per-season rate that he recently inked with the Kansas City Chiefs. And that's on the low end, as other quarterbacks like Caleb Williams and/or C.J. Stroud could balloon that market-setting figure this offseason with their looming extensions.

When you're talking about executing the largest contract in NFL history, there could be some trepidation depending on how Maye's ankle recovers. The Patriots have also historically been known to drag out talks, most recently not signing Christian Gonzalez to his market-setting deal until just before the start of the regular season. While waiting with Maye could give them further clarity on how his ankle heals, it also runs the risk of the price going up as other QBs sign their deals.

Drake Maye has also looked like two completely different quarterbacks over the course of this season. Through the first three games of the season, Maye was in the midst of an all-time-bad Super Bowl hangover. New England got off to a 1-2 start that saw the third-year quarterback throw six interceptions and put up the league's lowest quarterback rating of 58.6. Since then, though, Maye looked closer to last year's MVP-caliber run despite the Patriots' litany of injuries. Between Weeks 4 and 10, Maye ranked third in touchdown passes (17), fifth in completion percentage over expectation (plus-4.2%), second in success rate (51.1%), third in EPA per dropback (0.20), and second in yards per attempt (8.9) among 31 qualified quarterbacks, all while being bressured at the fourth-highest rate in the league (43.6%).

Possibly intertwined with Maye's extension could come some hard questions regarding who stays and who goes on this current version of the Patriots roster.

For instance, this offseason New England has receiver DeMario Douglas, offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, offensive lineman Michael Onwenu, safety Kevin Byard, linebacker Christian Elliss, and receiver Mack Hollins, all set to hit free agency. On top of that group, corner Carlton Davis (would create $16.5 million in cap space if cut), pass rusher Harold Landry ($14.5 million), and right tackle Morgan Mosses ($9 million) are all potential cut candidates to clear up space.

Each of those players mentioned is, or at least has been, a key contributor to the on-field product. Hollins and Douglas are the last two receivers on the roster who meaningfully contributed to the Patriots' 2024 Super Bowl Run; Onwenu has been New England's most reliable offensive lineman over the last few years; Byard currently leads the team in interceptions, while Ellis leads the team in tackles. New England will need to either look to the draft to fill those holes or dip their toe into the free-agent market.

At the moment, Over the Cap projects the Patriots to have roughly $16.8 million in available cap space.

There's really no other way to describe the A.J. Brown trade than as an utter disaster. When the Patriots shipped out a 2028 first-round pick as part of the blockbuster trade to acquire the star receiver, Brown was supposed to be the crown jewel that would take New England's offense to a new level. That hasn't materialized.

Brown has been limited to four games due to an array of injuries. He suffered a high ankle sprain early in the season, in the opening matchup against the Seattle Seahawks. That forced him on injured reserve. Then, after just two games back, a knee injury forced him to miss the club's Week 8 and Week 9 contests. To make matters even more maddening with Brown, he sufferd a third injury, leaving Sunday's Week 10 loss to the Lions early with a hamstring injury that will force him to miss multiple weeks.

So far, the wideout has suited up in four games and caught 11 of his 26 targets for 128 yards and zero touchdowns. Brown has also had three drops.

With Maye sidelined for the year, Brown faces immense pressure to produce when he's back on the field in 2027 and make last summer's sizable investment worth it. That could be a true roll of the dice, as Brown will be entering his age-30 season in 2027 and with a sizable injury history. He may not be the player he was during his early days in Tennessee or at the peak of his tenure in Philadelphia, but the Patriots will need more than what they've gotten from him next year.

If they don't, their record will likely suffer because of it and make that 2028 first-round pick that'll be awarded to the Eagles as part of the trade even more valuable.

While Drake Maye is still just 24 years old and hasn't even stepped into his prime yet, his team will be at a crossroads next year. The core they've built around Maye faces a make-or-break season that could lead to a reset if things continue to trend in the wrong direction.

For example, A.J. Brown is signed through 2029, but has no guaranteed money remaining on his contract in 2028 and 2029. If he doesn't turn a corner next year, it'd be hard to imagine New England re-upping him, and they would likely try to move on to clear space. Free-agent acquisition and fellow wideout Romeo Doubs is in the same boat as Brown. Those are two integral pieces to the offense that could be out the door quicker than they came in, and leave the organization looking for new pieces to surround Maye with, albeit now while paying him top dollar.

With the team not owning their own first-round pick in 2028 either, it only stresses the importance of these players (and others like them on the roster) finding their footing, as no blue-chippers are around the corner if they should struggle again in 2027.

#2634. The Timing Game – MH

von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar

The Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial. It not only allows pressing traps to be reversed but also enables teams to break down deep defensive blocks with precision. In the Premier League, Brighton’s then-manager Roberto De Zerbi took this tactical approach to a new level.

“Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola

The core idea of the Timing Game is to react to the opponent’s movement at precisely the right moment. Pressing traps can be reversed by first triggering and manipulating the opponent’s press and then bypassing it through changes in speed and direction. Since opposition pressing actions are highly dynamic, this approach is particularly effective against high-pressing teams. Consequently, the Timing Game allows teams to dominate pressing situations in their own buildup play. Additionally, because opponent movements can be triggered independently of the game phase, the Timing Game can also be applied against deep defensive blocks.

Regarding the role of timing in De Zerbi’s buildup play, René Maric (RM) explained in a 2023 interview with SkySports:

„The biggest thing in the build-up is the control of rhythm. If you look at Guardiola, he does it with the speed of the passes and then they carry the ball when they don’t have pressure. De Zerbi does it more with the moment of the pass, the lure, the sole on the ball, opening space with the pass rather than the carry. How you control the rhythm and progress through space will be big in the future. That development has already started.“

This article examines the dimensions and functioning of the Timing Game. Additionally, it analyzes the impact of a team’s own positioning, as well as the manipulation, anticipation, and triggering of the opponent’s press (or movements). The following sections will then explore the action of bypassing the opponent, the potential issues that arise within the Timing Game, and possible solutions to these challenges.

This section is an attempt to highlight the various facets of the Timing Game and football in general. Different playing philosophies prioritize different dimensions. In the Timing Game described here, particular focus is placed on the timing of dynamics in relation to the opponent.

To gain a better understanding of the principles of the Timing Game, the following section presents and explains its different dimensions. This makes it clear how the Timing Game differs from the focus of positional play and relationism but can also be combined with them. Although the game dimensions are less important for the practical implementation of the Timing Game, they can be useful for further developing this concept or other coaching philosophies.

The most important dimension of the Timing Game is the temporal dimension. The crucial factors are the speed and timing of decision-making. The timing of a progressive action should generally coincide with the opponent’s movement. The primary focus is therefore on the exact moment of an action.

A second important dimension is that of dynamics. The dynamic dimension of the Timing Game revolves around explosiveness and changes in rhythm. Changes in dynamics can be decisive both in relation to one’s own play and in terms of directional shifts in relation to the opponent. Ultimately, the goal is to create the strongest possible reciprocal acceleration in the opponent.

In the dimension of individual performance factors, the focus is on footballing competencies such as technical and athletic abilities. In the Timing Game, ball control is a crucial factor, as it significantly affects a player’s pressing resistance. Ball control involves both the ability to recognize a situation and the technical capability to handle the ball under pressure at any time. This skill is particularly important in the Timing Game, as it provides an advantage during the opponent’s pressing phase.

The causal-relational dimension deals with the cause-and-effect principle in interactions between teammates and opponents. There is a causal relationship both between the opponent’s defensive approach and the method of bypassing them, as well as between a teammate’s action and the resulting ball action. The following examples illustrate this:

In relationism, interactions between teammates are particularly emphasized to enable optimal interplay. Due to the complexity of this dimension, I have linked MR’s seminar “The Future of the Game” here.

In the spatial dimension, the focus is on controlling specific zones of the pitch. This is particularly crucial in positional play, where the aim is to control the game through ball possession and spatial occupation. In the Timing Game, however, the goal is to reach the space behind the opponent. Since this space is constantly changing, it cannot strictly be defined as a fixed pitch zone. However, the spatial dimension does play a role in the preparatory positioning of the Timing Game. This article contains a dedicated section on the optimal positioning in preparation for the Timing Game.

In the Timing Game, the moment of an action is primarily decisive. The moment of action is always triggered by the opponent’s movement. The more intense the opponent’s movement, the easier it is to bypass them. This is because, once the Timing Game is triggered, the opponent should be bypassed as diagonally opposed to their movement as possible. This forces the opponent into a maximal change of direction and dynamics.

The pressing near one’s own penalty area is bypassed diagonally opposite to the direction of the press.

A temporal advantage is created over the opponent, who initially has to accelerate in the opposite direction and loses time. The space that opens up behind the advancing opponent can be played most effectively. Representing the functioning of the Timing Game, the principle of “Lure and Shock” could be used. The opponent is first “lured” into the movement and then “shocked” by being bypassed.

The Timing Game is particularly effective during the opponent’s transition from a deeper to a higher pressing setup. At the moment of transition between ordered pressing phases, the opponent’s structure is often lacking, as the distances between the players change. Additionally, movement is present on all positions of the opponent, which can be exploited for the Timing Game. The direction of the opponent’s movement is also crucial, as during the transition from a deeper to a higher pressing phase, vertical movement away from the goal dominates, allowing spaces towards the opponent’s goal to be exploited.

This specific moment of the opponent’s pressing transition into a higher setup cannot be found in the classic phase model of the game according to Van Gaal. Depending on the perspective, it would be classified as part of either the team’s own possession phase or the opponent’s possession phase, even though it is significantly more complex and interesting than other possession situations. The opponent is essentially in a type of defensive transition into attack from the opponent’s ball possession, while the own team takes advantage of this moment and transitions from their own ball possession into a kind of offensive transition.

The Timing Game, however, does not only work during transitions between different pressing setups, but also independently of the game phase, and thus also within the framework of the opponent’s attacking press. The opponent’s movement in attacking pressing usually does not need to be triggered additionally. Instead, it is more about anticipating the moment when the opponent’s attacking press is triggered. At the moment of pressing initiation, there is a very high dynamic on multiple positions of the opponent in (diagonal) vertical directions, which allows the pressing to be bypassed with suitable movements at the moment of initiation. Particularly, the opponent’s pressing traps can be bypassed at the moment of initiation through a corresponding pre-rehearsed anticipation and movement.

Depending on the individual pressing patterns of the opponent, preparations should be made for the timing and manner of bypassing. For example, man-marking in attacking pressing can be bypassed differently than ball-oriented or hybrid marking schemes. Particularly against man-marking, it is important in the Timing Game to initially provoke dynamics in the opponent through various runs, in order to then bypass them in the opposite direction. If dynamics are not created through own runs, there is often little movement from the opponent in the second and third layers that could be exploited.

Because dynamics are also created in the opponent’s man-marking in the second and third layers, multiple layers can be bypassed.

The pressing triggers and pressing traps also differ depending on the type of attacking press, so anticipating the moments of the Timing Game requires prior analysis of the opponent. A very commonly used pressing trigger is a backward pass to the goalkeeper from a higher defensive line. A common reaction is for the goalkeeper to play the ball long under pressure, usually resulting in a loss of possession. In the Timing Game, a team would create passing options behind the opponent through collective movements at the moment the opponent triggers their press. Specific movements and methods for bypassing the press will be discussed in more detail later in the article.

Individual pressing patterns also include the opponent’s pressing structure itself. Here too, individual weaknesses can be diagnosed and exploited in advance. When the opponent presses from a 4-4-2, they often have an under-populated central area. Of course, this cannot be generalized, as, for example, the ball-far midfielder or an aggressive center-back may situationally reinforce the center. However, if this is not the case, an inverse run by the full-back at the moment the press is triggered could be useful to play into the space behind the press against the dynamics. It can be stated that the Timing Game, against different opponents with different individual pressing patterns, influences the movements made to bypass the press.

The Timing Game can also work against deep-lying opponents. However, it is more difficult here because, in general, there is less movement away from the goal, and the opponent attacks in a more passive manner. The deep-lying opponent’s goal is to close the space near the goal. It will be crucial to trigger the opponent’s movement or pressing and lure the opponent out. We will go into more detail on such trigger actions later.

In summary, the following rules for the Timing Game depending on the opponent’s pressing can be established: The deeper the opponent is positioned, the less dynamic movement there is away from their own goal. Therefore, the time window for bypassing the press is shorter. The more passive the opponent acts, the less frequently there is opponent movement. As a result, there will be fewer opportunities to bypass the press. Nevertheless, the Timing Game can be used independently of the game phase through trigger actions.

The team’s formation in possession should be adapted to the challenges of the Timing Game. It should create central connections through a vertical/diagonal alignment. This way, more layers can be incorporated into the dynamics, and more passing options can be created. More passing windows open up at the moment of triggering through a variety of passing angles. In the event of a loss of possession, it also allows for more effective counter-pressing.

Additionally, it can be useful to work with asymmetries and overloads. Overloading the own buildup zone is particularly effective when the opponent closes down and applies high pressure. This lures the opponent and allows them to be bypassed with a few passes. In the linked video example, De Zerbi’s Shakhtar Donetsk uses a strategy of having 7 players in their own penalty area during a goal kick to lure the opponent out.

Nothing to see here, just a completely normal build-up pic.twitter.com/vOcvRPVKdf

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) April 28, 2022

Problems in the Timing Game arise when there is an overload in the own buildup zone if the opponent does not press. The progression in the game is lacking because offensive passing options are not available. Also problematic is the static overload of the last line. If players remain in their specific spaces in the last line, passing options necessary to bypass the opponent’s press are missing.

Another way to structure the team to prepare for the Timing Game is by leaving a specific area vacant. If the opponent attempts to press, this space is usually left unoccupied by the opponent as well. Subsequently, the space can be attacked and played into from the second line in the opposite direction. If the space is still occupied, the numerical advantage in a ball-near area can be exploited. Real Madrid often employs such structures or space-drawing runs in preparation for their actual attacking play with the ball.

In the Timing Game, the moment the opponent begins to press must be anticipated as early as possible. Possible indicators for early recognition of a pressing moment include: the opponent’s approach towards the ball-carrying teammate, the shrinking of distances between the ball-near opponents and their teammates, and the forward dynamics of the opponent. A defensive line with equal numbers or an advancing defender is also an early recognition feature. Lastly, specific pressing triggers should be identified through video analysis in advance.

An exemplary player for effective pressing resistance is Sergio Busquets, who, with his excellent ball control, was regularly able to anticipate and resolve pressing situations. In this 2017 article, TR and MR wrote about Busquets’ qualities.

What is particularly interesting is triggering the opponent’s attacking press. There are a variety of very interesting trigger actions. One variation used by De Zerbi is the use of the sole on the ball to wait. This plays on the impatience of the opponent. The following quote and video clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this trigger action.

“It’s so fascinating to watch (…) when the ball goes to the center back, they freeze the game. (…) As soon as the pressing action happened, they then had this meticulously designed mechanism of up-back-throughs and third man connections (…).” – Jamie Hamilton, 3rd Circle Podcast

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) January 13, 2025

Another option is a pass triggered by speed. This pass should be played as slowly as possible and as quickly as necessary. The slow pass provokes the opponent’s pressing. At the same time, by the receiver moving towards the ball, the dynamics can immediately be reversed. This facilitates the transition into the action of bypassing or dribbling past the opponent. The pass direction should ideally be diagonal toward one’s own goal. This maximizes the reversal of dynamics.

Another approach is to play into the pressure, only to then “bounce” back into the direction of the opponent’s pressing path. The opponent is initially led to believe they have access by playing into the pressure. By bouncing the ball into the pressing direction, the opponent is forced to continue their run.

The classic way of forcing a passive opponent into movement is dribbling. The opponent is eventually made to press. However, it is also much harder to generate a dynamic shift and surprise effect, as the dribbling is already in the direction of play. Therefore, it is helpful if dribbling-skilled players attack the opponent in order to maintain the unpredictability of the next action with quick changes of direction. Alternatively, passes that bypass the opponent after dribbling in the opposite direction of the dribble path can create a dynamic shift in the opponent.

Against deep-lying opponents, the inside diagonal is a good method to force defenders on the last line to step out a few meters. When the ball is played diagonally from the outside to the center, the central defender steps out a few steps. This can be exploited in the opposite direction. The effect is enhanced by a player letting the ball pass, as immediately after, the defender’s back can be attacked. This move is known in relationism as Escadinha.

After the pressing trigger, the opponent should be bypassed through dynamic, diagonal directional changes. The direction of the first action should ideally not move away from the pressure but rather target, go over, or through it to attack the opponent’s movement. Instead of directly passing to the free player (e.g., the goalkeeper), a progressive, diagonal ball should be chosen.

To create passing options in the desired direction, specific movements are crucial. There are also various fundamental principles for this. The start of the ball action should be as late as possible but as early as necessary.

The timing of the movement of teammates should coincide with the moment the press begins, so they can be available to receive the ball under pressure, but not too early to avoid being caught by the opponent’s dynamic.

Dynamic movement should also be generated in the second and third layers to have the opportunity to bypass multiple layers. Otherwise, there is a risk of opponents from the second layer, who create covering shadows, not being affected by the opposing dynamic. In a less compact space behind the first pressing line, the dynamics can occur in stages, so the layers are played one after the other.

It is important that after an action, the next layer should be attacked immediately to maintain the dynamic.

The decisive action to overcome the opponent can be individual, group, or team tactical in nature. Below are specific examples of such actions.

A feint in the moment of pressing initiation can lead to bypassing the opponent. In the linked video, Musiala’s movement at the right moment leads to the goal. Although this movement is likely executed intuitively by Musiala at the right time, it can certainly be tactically repeated. The feint falls into the above-described phase of the pressing transition from a deeper to a higher pressing line, which is why Denmark’s player spacing is incorrect and the deep coverage is absent.

Brilliant angle of Jamal Musiala’s goal from last night. 🇩🇪#Germany #Denmark #Euro #Analysis pic.twitter.com/xl2MDgvXwb

Individually tactical, the first touch can be used both as a triggering action and as an overcoming action. By skillfully triggering the opponent’s movement, it may be enough to simply play the ball past the opponent or through their legs. The first touch is made as far as possible but as close as necessary to allow the player to regain possession of the ball immediately in front of the opponent. This is clearly seen at the very beginning of Woltemade’s first goal in the following video.

⚽#woltemade #u21 pic.twitter.com/mpdKiB4inJ

The no-look pass can also be a variant to surprise the opponent against the dynamics and running direction.

Florian Wirtz’s dribbles may initially seem unremarkable. However, upon closer observation, it becomes clear that Wirtz uses slight delays instead of flashy tricks to trigger the opponent’s movement, and then he moves the ball past the defender. This is also a form of timing play at the individual tactical level.

— thomassist (@thomassist25_) January 27, 2025

On the group tactical level, up-back-through (steil-klatsch) combinations are ideal for breaking into depth at the right moment. Here, the previously described positioning in preparation for the timing play is crucial. As many levels as possible should be occupied to open passing angles and options. The lay-off play has the advantage of being able to overcome the opponent with simple passes. It is remarkable how each of these passes is played against the opponent’s pressing direction, preventing the opponent from getting access to the ball.

— ファンキーヤング (@funkyyoung) November 19, 2024

Different variations of the play through the third man are also very effective. In the following video, the effectiveness can be admired at minute 0:13, using the example of the left center-back starting in the wrong direction.

Other possibilities in the group tactical area include one-twos against the dynamics, space-creating runs, counter movements, or dynamic zone rotations.

There are also team tactical variations for overcoming the opponent in the timing game. One such variation is playing the second ball directly into the backline with an appropriate zone overload at the moment the pressing is triggered. The preparatory positioning is the team tactical element here.

A team tactical counter movement could also be considered, where all players in the forward zones drop back, increasing the pressing distance to create more dynamic movement. At the same time, a player from the second line attacks deeply in the opposite direction.

One problem with the timing play is overcoming the covering shadow of the first pressing opponent. As the approaching opponent generates an increasingly larger covering shadow in a well-prepared pressing situation, passing options become limited. This can be solved through an individual tactical overcoming action, such as a dribble, a first touch, or others. Additionally, certain combination plays can help overcome the first pressing player. A back-up-back-through combination could be effective, where the first pass is played over a short distance to a nearby teammate (back), followed by an up-back-through combination to open new passing angles.

The short back pass to the goalkeeper, who has moved up into the defensive line, can bypass the covering shadow of the first pressing player.

Another problem could arise against teams with a very high pressing intensity. Since it is necessary to play into the pressure and trigger the pressing, one is systematically exposed to this high intensity repeatedly. However, this can also be used to one’s advantage. Opponents with high intensity also have high dynamics, which can be played against with greater effectiveness. Additionally, there is usually a high number of opponents in the attacking zones. Therefore, it is advisable to attack the farthest free space as directly as possible.

Hybrid pressing can also cause problems in the timings game. Since individual players act in specific spaces, responding situationally to regain possession of the ball, they do not necessarily carry the dynamics of the pressing players. As a result, they are more difficult to play past. However, certain off-ball runs could provide solutions here. One example would be the outside defender making a diagonal run into space far from the ball.

Lastly, there are issues when pressing the opponent during goal kicks. All playing philosophies face problems here, as the conditions to break out of the situation are not ideal. The ball is not in motion, the opponent can organize, and the playing field is limited by the goal line behind. Additionally, the risk is higher due to the proximity to the goal. The timings game would generate dynamics in the opponent by various runs from teammates, in order to reach the opponent’s back at the right moment.

The concept of dynamically timing a play to exploit the opponent’s movement at the right moment is already seen in practice. However, with a more deliberate approach, it can become more accessible to a wider range of players and even more effective. It holds the potential to bypass pressing traps and break down deep-lying defenses. It is not only applicable throughout the field but can also be effective with different numbers of players.

The dynamic timing play concept developed here is heavily focused on the reference point of the “opponent.” Another possible concept of timing could place more emphasis on the teammate, focusing on relational interactions between players. This concept would be more closely aligned with the relationalism theory. Using the dimensions outlined here, different game concepts can be created and further developed.

The timing play should be used as a complementary element to complete one’s overall playing philosophy. It provides a different perspective on tactical analysis than what would be possible with static graphics, such as those on a tactic board. Therefore, it should expand an analyst’s perspective on this complex game by adding an additional dimension.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

I know Pep Guardiola made De Zerbi the leading authority when it comes to the timing game but I also believe that Marcelino Garcia at Villarreal adds more layers to this topic. His understanding of dynamics is unique and is worth looking into.

#2633. White Sox add Dustin May on three-year, $52.5 million contract after Cinderella 2026 season, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The upstart Chicago White Sox have added one of the game's hardest-throwing pitchers to their rotation. Chicago and righty Dustin May have agreed to a three-year contract worth $52.5 million, reports FanSided.

May, 29, split this past season between the St. Louis Cardinals and World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers. He threw a career-high 145 ⅔ innings with a 4.70 ERA, though the underlying numbers (3.63 FIP and 4.50 expected ERA) were more respectable. May's 96.9 mph average fastball velocity was 15th highest among the 141 pitchers with at least 100 innings in 2026.

Rotation help was a priority for a White Sox team that reached the postseason for the first time since 2021, but used openers and bullpen games regularly throughout the season. Only twice in seven postseason games did Chicago use a traditional starting pitcher. Here is the team's updated rotation depth chart:

Castillo struggled badly (30 runs in 31 innings) after coming over from the Seattle Mariners at the trade deadline, and finished the season on the injured list with a shoulder issue. His $22.75 million salary could land him in the rotation on Opening Day, though the White Sox have enough options to replace him should Castillo remain ineffective.

We ranked May as the offseason's 25th-best free agent, and the 11th-best starting pitcher. Here's a snippet of the write-up:

May turned only 29 in September and he's topped 130 innings in back-to-back years after throwing 101 innings total around injuries, including UCL surgery, from 2021-24. Even after the injuries, May still lives in the mid-to-upper-90s with his sinker, and pitch data models are fond of his sweeper and curveball. It is not the best sign, though, that the Brewers, who know pitching as well as any team, couldn't fully unlock May after making him their big deadline rotation addition. Still, the combination of age and high-octane stuff makes him a nice upside play ...

May made two starts and three relief appearances during Milwaukee's postseason run. If the White Sox opt to use bullpen games again next year, he is familiar and capable in that role. The signing pushes Chicago's projected 2027 payroll up to $120 million, per FanGraphs, well above the team's $102 million figure this past season.

The White Sox went 84-78 in 2026 and became the first team in baseball history to reach the postseason after back-to-back 100-loss seasons. They lost 100 games in each of the three previous seasons, going 61-101 in 2023, 41-121 in 2024, and 60-102 in 2025.

#2630. Daniel Jones released by Colts: Why QB's contract almost ensures he'll clear waivers, be free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Daniel Jones era in Indianapolis didn't make it to the end of Year 2. The Colts cut their run with the veteran quarterback short, waiving him in the aftermath of a 26-3 defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in Week 11.

While cutting ties at this juncture was shocking for the Colts, a divorce seemed inevitable this offseason as the team is 3-8 with Jones as a main culprit of the organization's shortcomings. His 15 turnovers are the most in the NFL, and his 13 interceptions set a new career-high. Thursday's loss was also his sixth straight game with an interception, which is the longest streak by a Colts player since Curtis Painter in 2011.

That's not the version of Jones the Colts were hoping to get when they signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract extension back in March. They had hoped Jones would return to the player he was over the first eight games of the 2025 season, prior to suffering a season-ending Achilles tear. Over that stretch, Jones had the Colts at 7-1 while boasting a 109.5 passer rating. However, that flash in the pan was just that. Jones was unable to recapture that magic, and Indianapolis is now left paying a hefty price.

Below, we'll explain some financial ramifications regarding the Colts waiving Jones, what his contract says and why it'd be extremely surprising for a team to claim him before he clears waivers on Monday.

For 2027, the final year of Jones' extension, the quarterback was set to have a $46.8 million cap hit. By waiving him, Indy will actually clear about $11.6 million in space for this offseason as they look for a new signal-caller and replenish the roster. While there are cap savings, Jones will account for $35.2 million in dead money, which is tied to his $44 million signing bonus that was prorated through 2030, according to CBS Sports salary cap expert Joel Corry.

Again, this is assuming Jones is waived, which he almost certainly will be (we explain why below).

Meanwhile, Spotrac notes that Indy will have paid out $49.8 million to Jones for 11 games this season. Ouch.

Jones is now subject to waivers until Monday at 4 p.m. ET. Any team in the league can put in a claim for the veteran quarterback, but it's highly unlikely that'll be the case. Why? Any team that claims Jones would take on $2 million for the rest of this season and $38 million in non-guaranteed money in 2027, as noted by NFL Network.

When it comes to 2027, $6.5 million of Jones' base salary and a $4 million roster bonus are guaranteed for injury. So, any team claiming him off of waivers would be on the hook for at least $10.5 million next season.

It would be downright shocking to see any club electing to go down that route in a pursuit of Jones at this stage. If they're interested, the more cost-effective move would be for hiim to clear waivers, have the Colts pick up the tab, and sign him as a free agent at a lower number. Then, the hypothetical new team would only be responsible for whatever it signs him for.

Teams are calling the Rangers about left-hander MacKenzie Gore, who is a year away from free agency, according to The Athletic. There is some reluctance to trade for players with only one year of control because games could be lost to a work stoppage next year, but pitching is so in-demand that at least some clubs are exploring a deal for Gore.

Now 27, Gore is one of only six pitchers to make at least 30 starts in each of the last three years. His under-the-hood numbers (3.87 FIP and 4.19 expected ERA) were much better than his 4.58 actual ERA, plus he has long been considered to have untapped upside. Crawford, Houck, and Ovideo all missed significant time with injuries in 2026 (Crawford has not appeared in an MLB game since 2024) and are far down Boston's rotation depth chart. Skubal and agent Scott Boras will meet with the Blue Jays, Dodgers, Padres, and potentially two other teams in the coming days.

Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout and is therefore working on a tight schedule, much tighter than usual for top Boras clients. If Arozarena's market is slow to develop, perhaps New York would pounce.

Teams around the league believe the Rockies are more open to trading All-Star catcher Hunter Goodman now than they were at the trade deadline, reports MLB Network. Colorado is said to have set a very high asking price for Goodman, who in 2026 became just the tenth primary catcher with a 40-homer season. Ryan Jeffers and Carson Kelly represent viable free agent alternatives to Goodman as right-handed offense-first catchers, though Goodman is several years younger than both and will have a lower salary the next three years through arbitration. Teams will likely feel more confident in Goodman holding his production for another few years than Jeffers and Kelly.

#2627. Jerry Jones calls Cowboys 'a bad team'; says team has chance to play better after Christian Parker's demotion

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight teams have scored 26 or more points per game in the 2026 NFL season. The Buffalo Bills (31.9), the San Francisco 49ers (31.2), the Cincinnati Bengals (30.9), the Jacksonville Jaguars (29.9), the Dallas Cowboys (28.6), the Detroit Lions (28.6), the Chicago Bears (26.8), and the Kansas City Chiefs (26.3).

The Cowboys are the only team among those eight with more than two losses, and they have a 4-6 record. Dallas is one of only two teams with a scoring defense below league average, and theirs ranks 30th (28.2 points per game) out of the league's 32 teams. That's why Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones felt comfortably calling his squad "a bad team" on Friday.

"We have not been a good team and are a bad team," Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, via Yahoo Sports. "At 4-6, that says everything you need to say. ... Does that mean we will play a bad game [and] be a bad team on Sunday? Not necessarily. And that's why we're trying to improve."

One way the Cowboys tried to improve their ailing defense this week was to strip first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling duties and give them to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine. However, Parker will stay on with the team to run defensive meetings and build out the game plans, but the 34-year-old, the youngest defensive coordinator in Cowboys history, will not have the play-calling role defensive coordinators usually have on game day.

"We've got a chance to play better doing it this way," Jones said of Dallas' demotion of Parker, via The Dallas Morning News.

After Dallas allowed the 49ers to rack up 584 total yards, the most allowed in a Cowboys' home game in the 67-season history of the franchise, they now have the NFL's worst total defense (393.8 total yards per game allowed), run defense (154.1 rushing yards per game allowed), third down defense (48.8% third down conversion rate allowed) and the worst defense in terms of defensive expected points added (EPA) per play (-0.13).

To be fair to Dallas' coaching staff, many of the defensive issues the last few years have been with the players on the field. Per CBS Sports Research, the Cowboys are the only team in NFL history to allow 27-plus points per game in three consecutive seasons with a different defensive coordinator each year: Mike Zimmer (2024), Matt Eberflus (2025) and now Parker (2026). Nothing has stuck, which likely has more to do with Jones' roster-building and decision to trade away All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers.

Jones' and head coach Brian Schottenheimer's handling of Parker is very weird, but the move could at least get Dallas to a 6-6 record after Thanksgiving. Dallas hosts the 1-8 Tennessee Titans in Week 11, then takes on the 2-7 Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving Day.

#2626. Jake Bauers signs four-year, $58 million deal with Red Sox after helping lead Brewers to World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Boston Red Sox have made the offseason's first major free agent signing. The Red Sox and first baseman Jake Bauers have agreed to a four-year contract worth a reported $58 million, the team announced on Tuesday.

Bauers, 31, broke out with the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers this past season, authoring a .266/.389/.484 batting line with 26 home runs that more than doubled his previous career high (12). He was named the NLCS MVP during Milwaukee's title run thanks to a 4 for 14 (.286) effort. Bauers drove in seven runs in the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The Red Sox desperately needed a power bat and certainly added one with Bauers. Their 163 home runs this past season were the fifth fewest in baseball and three players -- Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Jarren Duran -- accounted for 71 of those 163 home runs. Boston's lineup figures to look something like this with Bauers now added:

That leaves Duran without a full-time position and makes a trade or even a non-tender more likely. Franklin Arias, one of the very best prospects in the minors, could debut early next season and wrestle the shortstop job away from Story. POBO Craig Breslow recently said Story is not locked in as the team's starting shortstop.

We ranked Bauers as the 12th-best free agent available this offseason, and the seventh-best position player free agent. Here's our write-up:

Rake Bauers (finally) lived up to the nickname this year and carried it over into the postseason, particularly during the NLCS. Long an exit velocity and hard-hit rate darling, Bauers fully tapped into his power in 2026 thanks to a more open stance and moving back in the box and further off the plate. That allowed him to see the ball better and get his bat into the hitting position on time more consistently. I'm not 100% sold on those adjustments solving his career-long issues with lefties, though at least there is a tangible reason to believe in his great left-on-left performance this season. Bauers can be an adventure in the field (he has played outfield in the past) and he just turned 31. A few teams will look for the next Jake Bauers rather than pay the actual Jake Bauers.

The Brewers tendered Bauers the $23.15 million qualifying offer and will receive a 2027 compensation draft pick after the first round because the contract exceeds $50 million. Because they paid the competitive balance tax, the Red Sox will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in bonus pool money for the 2027 international signing period, to sign Bauers.

Milwaukee could turn to Tyler Black and Andrew Vaughn at first base next season. Andrew Fischer, the No. 20 overall pick in the 2025 draft, slugged 48 home runs in the minors this summer and reached Double-A. He is the long-term solution at first base but is likely a year away from the big leagues. The Brewers could bring in a stopgap first baseman if they're not sold on Black.

The Red Sox went 87-75 this past season and were the second wild card team. They were swept by the rival New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series and scored only two runs in the two games.

#2624. Colts waive Daniel Jones: Indy not trading QB or Jonathan Taylor at deadline now a major second-guess

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Mobb Deep said it best: "Ain't no such thing as halfway crooks."

The Indianapolis Colts tried to sit on the fence at the 2026 trade deadline, ship away some (not all) expendable pieces, and land a somewhat respectable, middle-of-the-road record that might save a few jobs in the process. That meant moving on from the likes of DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson, and Josh Downs, but holding on to Jonathan Taylor and Daniel Jones. Less than two weeks removed from that semi-fire sale, it's safe to say Indy botched it.

What's the old saying? If you're going to be a bear, be a grizzly. Well, if the Colts felt alright selling some pieces at the deadline, they should've stripped it down to the studs, knowing full well they are entering a rebuild anyway after firing GM Chris Ballard in mid-October.

The losses have only continued to pile up for the Colts, which includes a demoralizing defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in Week 11. That game, which dropped them to 3-8, proved to be the straw that broke the camel's back for the Daniel Jones era, as the team has since waived the veteran quarterback.

Again, this is a player who teams were reportedly interested in leading up to the deadline. Instead of pursuing those opportunities to shed a sunk-cost under center, ESPN reports that Indy rebuffed trade interest from teams like the Minnesota Vikings and Baltimore Ravens.

As a reminder, the Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick to acquire Kirk Cousins, while the Ravens shipped a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-round pick to the Cardinals in exchange for Jacoby Brissett and a 2027 fifth-round pick. It's unclear what the compensation for Jones would've been, but I can tell you this—it's more than what they have now after waiving him: nothing.

In the nine games before the deadline, Jones had the Colts at 2-7 while completing 60.3% of his passes, averaging just 191.3 passing yards per game, and posting a passer rating of 68.9. In total, Jones had tallied seven touchdowns and 13 turnovers.

It was abundantly clear in the lead-up to the deadline that the two-year, $88 million extension the Colts signed Jones this offseason to was a disaster. Miraculously, a lifeboat drifted by them in the form of multiple teams inquiring about taking that burden off their hands, but they decided to stay on the deserted island. Now they're paying the price, with Jones set to account for $35.2 million in dead cap space for 2027 (provided he clears waivers) while the team pays him $49.8 million for 11 games played this season.

On top of Jones, Taylor, arguably the most sought-after prize on the trade market this cycle, should've been firmly on the block. With the Colts now without a clear answer at quarterback, Taylor is the living embodiment of that meme where the Lamborghini is sitting in the driveway of the trailer park.

He was most valuable to Indy as a trade chip at the deadline, and that remains the case this offseason. The only difference is that any team acquiring him is getting a back that's a little older, has a little more mileage, and doesn't help them for this stretch run in 2026. That sets up a possibly diminished return this offseason if/when the Colts deal him compared to what they could've gotten at this deadline.

For a team that won't have its first-round pick in 2027 after trading for Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, they were in a position to refill the cupboard. Neither Jones nor Taylor likely would've fetched a first-rounder, but they would've given Indy premium ammunition for a later deal that could vault them back up. That level of asset mismanagement around the deadline now has the potential to ripple beyond just this second half of the season.

Jones being waived is just one of the initial steps that the Colts will take as they embark on this rebuild and they tripped out of the gate. Whether it's firing Shane Steichen, trading Taylor, or eventually hiring a new GM (if they can find a taker), the organization needs to have a more definitive and realistic plan for its future so they're not looking back with major second guesses like they currently are following this deadline.

#2623. NBA Power Rankings: The LaMelo Ball effect is being felt in two places; Lakers take top spot from Spurs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards went down after four games, I ranked it as the biggest injury blow any team has suffered this season, which was saying a lot given all the injuries we've seen. As it turned out, Oklahoma City's barrage of injuries, Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Tyrese Haliburton in Indiana, Jaren Jackson Jr. in Utah, Paolo Banchero in Orlando, and now Stephen Curry with the Warriors have all turned out to be significantly more debilitating as Minnesota has gone 8-3 without Edwards.

How are they doing it? Let's take a look.

And by elite, we mean the best in the league. Minnesota is surrendering just 104 points per 100 possessions. Give Rudy Gobert his flowers, man. The Wolves' defensive rating drops to 97 points per 100 when he's on the court, while rising to 108.6 when he sits. That said, the Wolves have defenders everywhere you look and they are seriously tied together.

With their four regular starters on the floor (LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga and Gobert), Minnesota is registering a 92.0 defensive rating with a plus-20.5 net rating. But even when they go smaller and swap in Ayo Dosunmu for Gobert with the other three, the rating stays at 94.2 with a plus-16.2 net.

No matter the combination, if four of those five guys are on the court, the defense is no worse than 96.0. It's super impressive stuff, and so much for the idea that Ball is a defensive liability. Speaking of Ball ...

The LaMelo effect is being felt in two places: Minnesota, of course, but also Charlotte, where the offense has plummeted from a 123.3 rating with Ball on the court last year to a league-worst 103.1 this season. Being down Kon Knueppel doesn't help, but it's night and day watching this unit try to generate clean looks without Ball's creation and passing.

Meanwhile, the Wolves are flying. The defense is carrying the day and we're going to get to some of the guys carrying more impressive statistical weight than Ball, at least relatively, but watch this team play and try to argue his impact isn't all over the floor. He won the game for Minnesota on Tuesday with two defensive plays over the closing seconds.

LaMelo wins the game with back to back defensive plays! Who would have thought? 👀 pic.twitter.com/v9xYpR7eZu

Of course, his impact is felt most offensively. The pace. Energy. All of Minnesota's shooting percentages go up with Ball on the court, as they did last season in Charlotte, and that's not because of Ball's own shooting. He's only making 41.8% of his own shots, after all. It's his passing, his flow. As fancy as it is, it's fundamental in its contagious, force-multiplying impact.

The bottom line is this: Over his last 53 games between Charlotte and Minnesota, Ball has gone 39-14. That's the pace of a 60-win team. He's an agent of chaos, fine. It can look out of control. He still chucks up the playground shots, often off one foot and from barely inside the boundary. But we all wondered what it would look like when he was playing for a team with real stakes. Is he a winner? Or are his stats empty? Honestly, he's not even that impressive of a stats guy so far. He's just a winner.

The Wolves can deploy uncompromised lineups up and down their roster, meaning they don't have to decide between offense and defense. All their guys do both. They also have multiple offensive weapons even without Edwards, which is why Ball isn't having to carry a bigger scoring burden than he's equipped to handle, at least efficiently.

Terrence Shannon Jr. put up 34 off the bench in a win over Portland on Monday. The next night, Dosunmu and McDaniels, who are playing at legit All-Star levels, combined for 52 with nine 3-pointers. Kuminga is giving them 12.8 points, 5.7 rebounds, almost three assists and a steal over 30 minutes per game.

Other than Gobert, Jaylen Clark is really the only truly offensively limited guy, but for the minutes he gets, he is one hell of a defender. You do not want this man guarding you. You do not want anything to do with this team overall.

They came out of the gate looking incredible with Edwards and Ball looking like basketball brothers. It seemed like that was going to die out when Edwards got hurt. It hasn't.

When Edwards gets back, this Timberwolves team has the look of a legitimate contender.
